entities.name: Shark
entities.fact: Sharks have patrolled the oceans for more than 400 million years, and most species do their hunting at dusk and during the night.

entities.name: Dolphin
entities.fact: Dolphins hunt with echolocation, sending out clicks and reading the echoes to find fish even in murky water.

entities.name: Whale
entities.fact: Whales are mammals that breathe air through blowholes, and the baleen species strain krill and small fish through plates of keratin.

entities.name: Seal
entities.fact: True seals have no external ears and wriggle on land on their bellies, but underwater they can hold their breath for well over half an hour.

entities.name: Jellyfish
entities.fact: Jellyfish have drifted through the seas for more than 500 million years with no brain, heart or bones, and are about 95 percent water.

entities.name: Lobster
entities.fact: Lobsters hide in rocky dens by day, come out to hunt and scavenge at night, and regrow any claw or leg they lose.

entities.name: Octopus
entities.fact: Octopuses can regrow a lost arm complete with its suckers and nerves, and most species do their hunting at dusk and at night.

entities.name: Tuna
entities.fact: Tunas are warm-blooded fish that must swim constantly to breathe and can cross entire oceans in a few weeks.

entities.name: Salmon
entities.fact: Salmon hatch in rivers, grow up at sea and find their way back to their birth stream by smell to spawn.

entities.name: Butterflyfish
entities.fact: Butterflyfish are thin, brightly patterned reef fish, and many carry a false eye spot near the tail to confuse predators.

entities.name: Wrasse
entities.fact: Wrasses are among the most varied reef fish families, and many change from female to male partway through life.

entities.name: Triggerfish
entities.fact: A triggerfish locks its first dorsal spine upright to wedge itself into a crevice, and only the small second spine, the trigger, can release it.

entities.name: Pufferfish
entities.fact: Pufferfish inflate with water to deter predators and carry tetrodotoxin, a poison with no known antidote.

entities.name: Saltwater crocodile
entities.fact: The saltwater crocodile, the largest living reptile, swims between islands across the eastern Indian Ocean and has been found hundreds of kilometres out to sea.

entities.name: Mid-Atlantic Ridge
entities.fact: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge is a chain of underwater volcanoes where new seafloor forms as Europe and Africa drift away from the Americas.

entities.name: Mariana Trench
entities.fact: The Mariana Trench holds the deepest point of any ocean, Challenger Deep, at roughly 10,935 metres below the surface.

entities.name: Challenger Deep
entities.fact: Challenger Deep, the floor of the Mariana Trench, was first reached by Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh in the bathyscaphe Trieste in 1960.

entities.name: Puerto Rico Trench
entities.fact: The Puerto Rico Trench is the deepest part of the Atlantic Ocean, dropping to more than 8,000 metres at the Milwaukee Deep.

entities.name: Tonga Trench
entities.fact: The Tonga Trench is the second-deepest trench on Earth, and its Horizon Deep lies more than 10,800 metres down.

entities.name: Grand Banks
entities.fact: The Grand Banks off Newfoundland are shallow underwater plateaus whose cod fishery fed Europe for centuries before collapsing in 1992.

entities.name: Dogger Bank
entities.fact: Dogger Bank is a large sandbank in the middle of the North Sea that was dry land, part of Doggerland, when sea levels were lower after the last ice age.

entities.name: Georges Bank
entities.fact: Georges Bank is a shallow, fish-rich bank between Cape Cod and Nova Scotia that was once above sea level and later disputed between the USA and Canada.

entities.name: Stellwagen Bank
entities.fact: Stellwagen Bank, a sandy plateau at the mouth of Massachusetts Bay, is a national marine sanctuary famous for its humpback whale watching.

entities.name: Monterey Canyon
entities.fact: Monterey Canyon off California is a submarine canyon comparable in scale to the Grand Canyon, plunging to more than 3,000 metres.

entities.name: Hudson Canyon
entities.fact: Hudson Canyon is the largest submarine canyon on the US Atlantic coast, continuing the course of the Hudson River across the seabed off New York.

entities.name: East Pacific Rise
entities.fact: The East Pacific Rise is a fast-spreading mid-ocean ridge where the first black-smoker hydrothermal vents were discovered in 1979.

entities.name: Juan de Fuca Ridge
entities.fact: The Juan de Fuca Ridge off the Pacific Northwest is a spreading ridge whose vents are wired to shore by a cabled seafloor observatory.

entities.name: Hawaiian-Emperor seamount chain
entities.fact: The Hawaiian-Emperor seamount chain is a line of drowned volcanoes stretching about 6,000 kilometres across the Pacific, built as the plate moved over a hotspot.

entities.name: Loihi Seamount
entities.fact: Loihi, now officially Kamaʻehuakanaloa, is an active undersea volcano south-east of Hawaii that may one day grow into the next Hawaiian island.

entities.name: Davidson Seamount
entities.fact: Davidson Seamount off central California is a huge extinct volcano whose deep flanks hold forests of ancient corals and an 'octopus garden' of brooding mothers.

entities.name: Bowie Seamount
entities.fact: Bowie Seamount off British Columbia rises from about 3,000 metres to within roughly 25 metres of the surface and is a Canadian marine protected area.

entities.name: Cobb Seamount
entities.fact: Cobb Seamount, about 500 kilometres off Washington State, is a flat-topped underwater volcano whose summit lies just a few dozen metres below the surface.

entities.name: New England Seamounts
entities.fact: The New England Seamounts are a chain of extinct volcanoes running south-east from Georges Bank into the deep Atlantic, home to cold-water coral gardens.

entities.name: Great Bahama Bank
entities.fact: The Great Bahama Bank is a vast limestone platform so shallow that its turquoise waters are plainly visible from space, with the Tongue of the Ocean cut into it.

entities.name: Walvis Ridge
entities.fact: The Walvis Ridge is a long volcanic ridge running from the Namibian coast towards Tristan da Cunha, formed by a hotspot as the South Atlantic opened.

entities.name: Ninety East Ridge
entities.fact: The Ninety East Ridge is a remarkably straight underwater mountain chain in the Indian Ocean, named because it follows the 90th meridian east.

entities.name: Kerguelen Plateau
entities.fact: The Kerguelen Plateau in the southern Indian Ocean is one of the largest submerged volcanic plateaus on Earth, with only a few island peaks breaking the surface.

entities.name: Lomonosov Ridge
entities.fact: The Lomonosov Ridge crosses the Arctic Ocean floor near the North Pole and is claimed by Russia, Canada and Denmark in competing seabed submissions.

entities.name: Gakkel Ridge
entities.fact: The Gakkel Ridge beneath the Arctic ice is the slowest-spreading mid-ocean ridge known, yet it still hosts active hydrothermal vents.

entities.name: Reykjanes Ridge
entities.fact: The Reykjanes Ridge is the stretch of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge that runs south-west from Iceland, where the ridge actually rises above sea level.

entities.name: Chatham Rise
entities.fact: The Chatham Rise is a broad submarine plateau east of New Zealand that supports one of the country's most important fishing grounds, including hoki.

entities.name: Zealandia
entities.fact: Zealandia is a continent-sized block of crust around New Zealand of which about 94 percent lies underwater, drowned after it split from Gondwana.

entities.name: Great Blue Hole
entities.fact: The Great Blue Hole off Belize is a near-circular sinkhole about 300 metres across and 120 metres deep that was a dry cave before the sea rose.

entities.name: Dragon Hole
entities.fact: The Dragon Hole in the South China Sea is the deepest known blue hole, reaching roughly 300 metres down into the reef.

entities.name: Lost City hydrothermal field
entities.fact: The Lost City is a field of pale carbonate chimneys up to 60 metres tall on the Atlantis Massif in the mid-Atlantic, venting warm alkaline fluid rather than black smoke.

entities.name: Rockall Bank
entities.fact: Rockall Bank is a submerged plateau west of Scotland from which only the tiny granite islet of Rockall breaks the surface.

entities.name: Porcupine Bank
entities.fact: Porcupine Bank, west of Ireland, is a raised area of seabed named after HMS Porcupine, the survey ship that charted it in the 1860s.

entities.name: Flemish Cap
entities.fact: The Flemish Cap is an underwater plateau east of the Grand Banks, a fishing ground immortalised in the film The Perfect Storm.

entities.name: Sunda Shelf
entities.fact: The Sunda Shelf is the drowned extension of mainland South-east Asia, shallow seafloor that linked Borneo, Sumatra and Java to the continent during ice ages.

entities.name: Java Trench
entities.fact: The Java Trench, also called the Sunda Trench, is the deepest point of the Indian Ocean at more than 7,000 metres and marks the subduction zone that produced the 2004 tsunami.

entities.name: Great Barrier Reef Marine Park
entities.fact: The Great Barrier Reef Marine Park protects about 344,000 square kilometres of reef off Queensland, the largest coral reef system on Earth.

entities.name: Galápagos Marine Reserve
entities.fact: The Galápagos Marine Reserve covers well over 130,000 square kilometres around the islands and is famous for schooling hammerheads and marine iguanas.

entities.name: Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary
aliases: John Pennekamp Coral Reef State Park
entities.fact: The Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary protects the only living coral barrier reef in the continental United States.

entities.name: Monterey Bay National Marine Sanctuary
entities.fact: Monterey Bay National Marine Sanctuary stretches along central California and shelters kelp forests, sea otters and a submarine canyon deeper than the Grand Canyon.

entities.name: Raja Ampat
entities.fact: Raja Ampat in Indonesian West Papua lies at the heart of the Coral Triangle and holds more reef fish and coral species than almost anywhere else on Earth.

entities.name: Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument
entities.fact: Papahānaumokuākea protects the uninhabited north-western Hawaiian Islands and is one of the largest marine protected areas in the world.

entities.name: Ningaloo Marine Park
entities.fact: Ningaloo Reef in Western Australia is a fringing reef you can swim to from the beach, famous for whale sharks that gather every autumn.

entities.name: Ross Sea Marine Protected Area
entities.fact: The Ross Sea Marine Protected Area in Antarctica, agreed in 2016, is among the largest protected areas on the planet and shelters Adélie penguins and toothfish.

entities.name: Chagos Marine Protected Area
entities.fact: The Chagos Archipelago in the Indian Ocean was declared a no-take marine reserve in 2010 around some of the cleanest coral reefs in the world.

entities.name: Bonaire National Marine Park
entities.fact: Bonaire's entire coastline has been a marine park since 1979, and divers simply walk in from shore to reach its reefs.

entities.name: Sipadan
entities.fact: Sipadan, off Malaysian Borneo, is an oceanic island rising 600 metres from the seabed, famed for green turtles and swirling barracuda tornadoes.

entities.name: Blue Corner
entities.fact: Blue Corner in Palau is a current-swept reef wall where divers hook onto the rock to watch sharks and schooling fish stream past.

entities.name: Ras Mohammed National Park
entities.fact: Ras Mohammed, Egypt's first national park, sits at the tip of the Sinai where the Red Sea's Shark Reef and Yolanda Reef draw divers from around the world.

entities.name: SS Thistlegorm
entities.fact: The SS Thistlegorm, a British freighter sunk in the Red Sea in 1941, still holds motorbikes, trucks and locomotives and is among the most dived wrecks anywhere.

entities.name: Silfra
entities.fact: Silfra in Iceland is a flooded crack between the North American and Eurasian plates, with glacial water so clear that visibility exceeds 100 metres.

entities.name: Komodo National Park
entities.fact: Komodo National Park in Indonesia protects not only its dragons but strong-current reefs where manta rays gather to be cleaned.

entities.name: Cocos Island
entities.fact: Cocos Island, about 550 kilometres off Costa Rica, is a World Heritage site where divers come for huge schools of scalloped hammerheads.

entities.name: Darwin's Arch
entities.fact: Darwin's Arch in the northern Galápagos was a natural rock arch above a legendary hammerhead dive site until it collapsed into the sea in 2021.

entities.name: Malpelo Island
entities.fact: Malpelo, a bare rock in the Colombian Pacific, is a sanctuary where hundreds of hammerheads and silky sharks gather around its steep walls.

entities.name: Revillagigedo Archipelago
entities.fact: The Revillagigedo Islands, often just called Socorro, are a Mexican national park where giant oceanic manta rays approach divers to be cleaned.

entities.name: Tubbataha Reefs Natural Park
entities.fact: Tubbataha, two coral atolls in the middle of the Sulu Sea in the Philippines, can only be dived by liveaboard for a few months each year.

entities.name: Bunaken National Park
entities.fact: Bunaken, off Sulawesi in Indonesia, is known for coral walls that drop almost vertically into deep water right beside the shore.

entities.name: Poor Knights Islands
entities.fact: The Poor Knights Islands off New Zealand's North Island are a marine reserve that Jacques Cousteau rated among the best dive sites in the world.

entities.name: Dean's Blue Hole
entities.fact: Dean's Blue Hole in the Bahamas plunges to about 200 metres from a shallow beach and is a favourite venue for world-record freediving.

entities.name: SS Yongala
entities.fact: The SS Yongala sank in a cyclone off Queensland in 1911 with everyone aboard, and the wreck is now smothered in corals and giant groupers.

entities.name: USS Liberty wreck
entities.fact: The USS Liberty, torpedoed in 1942 and pushed into the sea by a volcanic eruption in 1963, lies just off the beach at Tulamben in Bali.

entities.name: Molokini
entities.fact: Molokini is a crescent-shaped volcanic crater off Maui whose sheltered inner reef is one of Hawaii's most visited snorkelling spots.

entities.name: Cabo Pulmo National Park
entities.fact: Cabo Pulmo in Baja California saw its fish biomass rise more than fourfold within a decade after fishing was banned, a celebrated conservation success.

entities.name: Richelieu Rock
entities.fact: Richelieu Rock, a horseshoe-shaped pinnacle in the Andaman Sea off Thailand, is prized for whale shark sightings and purple soft corals.

entities.name: Aliwal Shoal
entities.fact: Aliwal Shoal off South Africa's KwaZulu-Natal coast is famous for baited dives with tiger sharks and the winter gathering of ragged-tooth sharks.

entities.name: Pelagos Sanctuary
aliases: Pelagos Sanctuary for Mediterranean Marine Mammals
entities.fact: The Pelagos Sanctuary is a marine mammal reserve between France, Monaco and Italy where fin whales and striped dolphins feed in the Ligurian Sea.

entities.name: Phoenix Islands Protected Area
entities.fact: The Phoenix Islands Protected Area in Kiribati covers more than 400,000 square kilometres of the central Pacific around eight coral atolls.

entities.name: Marianas Trench Marine National Monument
entities.fact: The Marianas Trench Marine National Monument protects the waters and seabed around the deepest trench on Earth and its mud volcanoes.

entities.name: Palau National Marine Sanctuary
entities.fact: Palau closed about 80 percent of its waters to fishing in 2020, creating one of the largest fully protected marine sanctuaries in the world.

entities.name: Dahab Blue Hole
entities.fact: The Blue Hole at Dahab in Egypt is a 100-metre-deep sinkhole in the Red Sea reef whose deep arch has claimed many divers' lives.

entities.name: Cozumel Reefs National Park
entities.fact: Cozumel's reefs off Mexico's Yucatán are known for drift diving, where the current carries divers along walls such as Palancar and Santa Rosa.

entities.name: Hanauma Bay
entities.fact: Hanauma Bay on Oahu is a flooded volcanic crater that became Hawaii's first marine life conservation district in 1967.

entities.name: Channel Islands National Marine Sanctuary
entities.fact: The Channel Islands National Marine Sanctuary off southern California protects kelp forests where cold northern and warm southern currents meet.

entities.name: Scapa Flow
entities.fact: Scapa Flow in Orkney is where the interned German High Seas Fleet was scuttled in 1919, leaving battleships and cruisers that divers still explore.

entities.name: Sea turtle
entities.fact: Sea turtles return to lay their eggs on the same stretch of beach where they hatched, navigating partly by sensing Earth's magnetic field.

entities.name: Hawksbill sea turtle
entities.fact: The hawksbill is critically endangered, hunted for centuries for the patterned shell that was sold as 'tortoiseshell'.

entities.name: Green sea turtle
entities.fact: The green sea turtle is named for the green colour of its body fat, which comes from a diet of seagrass and algae.

entities.name: Leatherback sea turtle
entities.fact: The leatherback is the largest turtle alive, and its Pacific populations are critically endangered after collapsing by more than 90 percent.

entities.name: Loggerhead sea turtle
entities.fact: Loggerhead turtles nest on Gulf of Mexico and Florida beaches and use their powerful jaws to crush conchs and crabs.

entities.name: Kemp's ridley sea turtle
entities.fact: Kemp's ridley, the rarest sea turtle, nests almost entirely on one stretch of Gulf of Mexico beach in Mexico, coming ashore in daytime mass arrivals.

entities.name: Olive ridley sea turtle
entities.fact: Olive ridleys come ashore in their hundreds of thousands at once on beaches in Odisha, India, in mass nestings called arribadas.

entities.name: Whale shark
entities.fact: The whale shark is the largest fish alive, yet it is listed as endangered after its numbers fell by more than half over three generations.

entities.name: Great white shark
entities.fact: Great white sharks can sense the tiny electrical fields given off by a hidden animal's heartbeat.

entities.name: Hammerhead shark
entities.fact: A hammerhead's wide head spreads its eyes and electrical sensors apart, giving it a wider sweep of the seabed when hunting stingrays.

entities.name: Scalloped hammerhead
entities.fact: Scalloped hammerheads gather in schools of hundreds around seamounts and islands such as the Galápagos, and are critically endangered.

entities.name: Great hammerhead
entities.fact: The great hammerhead, the largest of its family, is critically endangered because its big fins are prized in the fin trade.

entities.name: Tiger shark
entities.fact: Tiger sharks are named for the dark stripes on young animals and do much of their hunting at night, when they move into shallow water.

entities.name: Bull shark
entities.fact: Bull sharks can live in fresh water and have been found far up the Mississippi and Amazon rivers and in Lake Nicaragua.

entities.name: Nurse shark
entities.fact: Nurse sharks spend the day resting in piles on the Caribbean seabed and hunt at night, sucking prey out of crevices.

entities.name: Whitetip reef shark
entities.fact: Whitetip reef sharks rest in caves by day and hunt at night, wriggling into reef crevices after sleeping fish.

entities.name: Blacktip reef shark
entities.fact: The blacktip reef shark patrols shallow Indo-Pacific reef flats, and its black-tipped dorsal fin is often seen cutting the surface.

entities.name: Grey reef shark
entities.fact: Grey reef sharks give a hunched, exaggerated warning display before they will bite, a famous threat posture among sharks.

entities.name: Caribbean reef shark
entities.fact: The Caribbean reef shark is the most common large shark on Caribbean reefs and the star of shark-feeding dives in the Bahamas.

entities.name: Galápagos shark
entities.fact: The Galápagos shark was first described from the islands but actually lives around oceanic islands across the tropics.

entities.name: Silky shark
entities.fact: The silky shark, named for its smooth skin, gathers in large numbers around the Galápagos, Cocos and Malpelo islands.

entities.name: Oceanic whitetip shark
entities.fact: The oceanic whitetip was once among the most abundant large sharks in the open ocean but is now critically endangered.

entities.name: Basking shark
entities.fact: The basking shark, second-largest fish on Earth, filters plankton from British and North Sea waters each summer and is listed as endangered.

entities.name: Shortfin mako
entities.fact: The shortfin mako is the fastest shark and was listed as endangered in 2019 after heavy fishing across the Atlantic.

entities.name: Sand tiger shark
entities.fact: The sand tiger shark looks fierce but is docile, hunts at night, and is critically endangered because it produces only one or two pups every two years.

entities.name: Angelshark
entities.fact: The angelshark, a flat shark that ambushes prey from the sand at night, has vanished from most of its European range and is critically endangered.

entities.name: Spiny dogfish
entities.fact: The spiny dogfish, a small North Sea and Pacific shark with venomous spines, has one of the longest pregnancies of any animal at up to two years.

entities.name: Bluntnose sixgill shark
entities.fact: The sixgill shark keeps six gill slits like sharks from the age of the dinosaurs and rises from the deep at night to feed.

entities.name: Frilled shark
entities.fact: The frilled shark, with its eel-like body and 300 needle teeth, belongs to a lineage that has changed little in about 80 million years.

entities.name: Goblin shark
entities.fact: The goblin shark is the only living member of a family dating back about 125 million years, and it shoots its jaws forward to snatch prey.

entities.name: Orca
entities.fact: Orcas are the largest dolphins, and the resident pods of the Pacific Northwest live almost entirely on salmon.

entities.name: Bottlenose dolphin
entities.fact: Bottlenose dolphins are the dolphins most often seen along the Gulf of Mexico and Caribbean coasts, and some pods chase fish onto mud banks and slide after them.

entities.name: Spinner dolphin
entities.fact: Spinner dolphins leap and spin up to seven times in the air, and rest in sheltered bays by day before hunting offshore at night.

entities.name: Humpback whale
entities.fact: Humpback whales sing songs that can last for hours, and all the males in one ocean region sing the same slowly changing tune.

entities.name: Blue whale
entities.fact: The blue whale is the largest animal ever known to have lived, and it remains endangered after whaling removed the great majority of its numbers.

entities.name: Sperm whale
entities.fact: Sperm whales dive more than a kilometre down to hunt squid and have the largest brain of any animal.

entities.name: Grey whale
entities.fact: Grey whales migrate along the Pacific coast of North America between Alaska and Mexico, a round trip of roughly 16,000 to 20,000 kilometres.

entities.name: Minke whale
entities.fact: The minke whale is the smallest of the rorquals and the baleen whale most often seen in the North Sea.

entities.name: Sei whale
entities.fact: The sei whale, one of the fastest great whales, is endangered after heavy whaling in the 1960s and 1970s.

entities.name: North Atlantic right whale
entities.fact: Fewer than about 400 North Atlantic right whales remain, and ship strikes and fishing-gear entanglement are their main killers.

entities.name: Harbour porpoise
entities.fact: The harbour porpoise is the most common cetacean in the North Sea and the only one that breeds in the Baltic Sea.

entities.name: Vaquita
entities.fact: The vaquita, a tiny porpoise found only in the upper Gulf of California, is the most endangered marine mammal, with perhaps ten or so individuals left.

entities.name: Hector's dolphin
entities.fact: Hector's dolphin, found only around New Zealand, is one of the smallest dolphins and is endangered mainly because of gillnet drownings.

entities.name: Māui dolphin
entities.fact: The Māui dolphin, a subspecies of Hector's dolphin off New Zealand's North Island, numbers only about 50 adults.

entities.name: Irrawaddy dolphin
entities.fact: The Irrawaddy dolphin lives in coastal waters and rivers from India to Indonesia and is endangered, with tiny isolated river populations.

entities.name: Yangtze finless porpoise
entities.fact: The Yangtze finless porpoise is the only freshwater porpoise and is critically endangered, with roughly 1,000 animals left in the river.

entities.name: Ganges river dolphin
entities.fact: The Ganges river dolphin is almost blind and finds fish in muddy water by echolocation, and it is listed as endangered.

entities.name: Sea otter
entities.fact: Sea otters have the densest fur of any animal and are endangered, having been hunted almost to extinction for it by the early 1900s.

entities.name: Sea lion
entities.fact: Sea lions differ from true seals in having external ear flaps and front flippers strong enough to walk on land.

entities.name: Steller sea lion
entities.fact: The Steller sea lion, the largest of the sea lions, breeds on rocky shores from California to Alaska and across to Russia.

entities.name: Galápagos sea lion
entities.fact: The Galápagos sea lion is endangered, its numbers swinging sharply when El Niño warms the water and drives away its fish.

entities.name: Galápagos fur seal
entities.fact: The Galápagos fur seal is the smallest fur seal and the only one living on the equator, and it is listed as endangered.

entities.name: Australian sea lion
entities.fact: The Australian sea lion is endangered and has an unusual 17- to 18-month breeding cycle found in no other seal.

entities.name: Hawaiian monk seal
entities.fact: The Hawaiian monk seal is endangered, with only about 1,500 animals, most of them in the remote north-western Hawaiian Islands.

entities.name: Harbour seal
entities.fact: The harbour seal hauls out on sandbanks and rocky shores on both sides of the North Atlantic and North Pacific, and in the North and Baltic seas.

entities.name: Grey seal
entities.fact: About 40 percent of the world's grey seals breed around Britain, and the North Sea population has grown strongly since hunting stopped.

entities.name: Ringed seal
entities.fact: The ringed seal is the smallest Arctic seal, and an isolated population breeds on the winter sea ice of the Baltic Sea.

entities.name: Northern elephant seal
entities.fact: Northern elephant seals were reduced to fewer than 100 animals by the 1890s but now breed in the tens of thousands on Californian and Mexican beaches.

entities.name: West Indian manatee
entities.fact: West Indian manatees graze on seagrass in the Caribbean and Gulf of Mexico and gather in Florida's warm springs each winter.

entities.name: Dugong
entities.fact: The dugong is the only strictly marine sirenian and grazes seagrass meadows across the Indian Ocean from East Africa to Australia.

entities.name: Marine iguana
entities.fact: The marine iguana of the Galápagos is the only lizard that feeds in the sea, diving to graze algae and sneezing out the excess salt.

entities.name: Galápagos penguin
entities.fact: The Galápagos penguin is the only penguin living on the equator and is endangered, with fewer than about 2,000 birds.

entities.name: African penguin
entities.fact: The African penguin of South Africa and Namibia was declared critically endangered in 2024 as its sardine and anchovy prey dwindled.

entities.name: Blue-footed booby
entities.fact: Blue-footed boobies plunge-dive into Galápagos waters for fish, and males show off their blue feet in a high-stepping courtship dance.

entities.name: Flightless cormorant
entities.fact: The flightless cormorant of the Galápagos has stubby wings and swims after fish and octopus along the shore, the only cormorant unable to fly.

entities.name: Giant manta ray
entities.fact: The giant manta ray can span about 7 metres across and was listed as endangered in 2020 because of fishing for its gill plates.

entities.name: Reef manta ray
entities.fact: Reef manta rays gather by the hundreds at Hanifaru Bay in the Maldives to feed on plankton swept in by the monsoon.

entities.name: Munk's devil ray
entities.fact: Munk's devil rays gather in schools of thousands off Baja California and the Galápagos and leap metres into the air, landing with a slap.

entities.name: Spotted eagle ray
entities.fact: The spotted eagle ray glides over Caribbean and Galápagos reefs on wing-like fins and digs clams out of the sand with its duck-like snout.

entities.name: Stingray
entities.fact: Stingrays bury themselves in sand and defend themselves with a serrated venomous spine at the base of the tail.

entities.name: Southern stingray
entities.fact: Southern stingrays at Stingray City in the Cayman Islands have learned to gather in the shallows where snorkellers hand-feed them squid.

entities.name: Cownose ray
entities.fact: Cownose rays migrate in schools of thousands along the Gulf of Mexico and US Atlantic coasts, their wingtips breaking the surface.

entities.name: Bat ray
entities.fact: The bat ray of the Californian coast flaps along the bottom of bays and kelp forests, digging up clams with its wings and snout.

entities.name: Smalltooth sawfish
entities.fact: The smalltooth sawfish is critically endangered and in the USA survives mainly in south-west Florida and the Gulf of Mexico.

entities.name: Thornback ray
entities.fact: The thornback ray is the skate most often caught around Britain, and its empty egg cases wash up on North Sea beaches as 'mermaid's purses'.

entities.name: Giant Pacific octopus
entities.fact: The giant Pacific octopus of the North American Pacific coast is the largest octopus, with an arm span that can exceed 4 metres.

entities.name: Caribbean reef octopus
entities.fact: The Caribbean reef octopus shimmers blue-green and hunts at night, spreading its webbed arms over coral heads like a parachute to trap prey.

entities.name: Humboldt squid
entities.fact: Humboldt squid rise from the deep at night in packs to hunt, flashing red and white, and have spread north along the Pacific coast to Alaska.

entities.name: Hawaiian bobtail squid
entities.fact: The Hawaiian bobtail squid hunts at night and hides its silhouette from predators below by glowing with light from bacteria housed in its body.

entities.name: Market squid
entities.fact: Market squid gather in vast spawning schools off California, supporting one of the state's most valuable fisheries.

entities.name: Vampire squid
entities.fact: The vampire squid is the last survivor of an ancient order that is neither squid nor octopus, drifting in oxygen-poor deep water eating falling 'marine snow'.

entities.name: Common cuttlefish
entities.fact: The common cuttlefish of the North Sea and Mediterranean changes colour in a split second and can regrow damaged arms.

entities.name: Squid
entities.fact: Squid use jet propulsion, and several species can regrow lost tentacles and arm tips.

entities.name: Nautilus
entities.fact: The nautilus is a shelled cephalopod whose lineage has barely changed in about 500 million years, adjusting gas in its chambers to float.

entities.name: Queen conch
entities.fact: The queen conch grazes Caribbean seagrass beds and hops along on a claw-shaped foot, and its pink shell is a souvenir on every island.

entities.name: Flamingo tongue
entities.fact: The flamingo tongue is a small Caribbean snail whose leopard-spotted colours are on a living mantle wrapped over a plain white shell, and it eats sea fans.

entities.name: Giant clam
entities.fact: The giant clam can weigh more than 200 kilograms and farms algae in its colourful mantle for much of its food.

entities.name: Cone snail
entities.fact: Cone snails hunt at night, harpooning fish with a venomous tooth, and some species can kill a human.

entities.name: Blue mussel
entities.fact: Blue mussels carpet rocky shores and sandbanks of the North and Baltic seas, anchored by tough threads they spin themselves.

entities.name: Eastern oyster
entities.fact: The eastern oyster builds reefs along the Gulf of Mexico, and the Gulf produces most of the oysters eaten in the United States.

entities.name: Geoduck
entities.fact: The geoduck of the Pacific Northwest is the largest burrowing clam, with a siphon up to a metre long, and can live well over 100 years.

entities.name: Gumboot chiton
entities.fact: The gumboot chiton, nicknamed the wandering meatloaf, is the largest chiton in the world and grazes algae along the North American Pacific coast.

entities.name: Moon snail
entities.fact: The moon snail ploughs through Pacific Northwest sand flats and drills a neat round hole in clam shells to eat them.

entities.name: Caribbean spiny lobster
entities.fact: Caribbean spiny lobsters hide in reef crevices by day, hunt at night, and migrate in single-file lines of dozens across the sand in autumn.

entities.name: American lobster
entities.fact: The American lobster forages mostly at night and can drop a claw to escape, then regrow it over several moults.

entities.name: European lobster
entities.fact: The European lobster is blue-black alive and only turns red when cooked, and it lives in rocky North Sea and Atlantic seabeds.

entities.name: Norway lobster
entities.fact: The Norway lobster lives in burrows on muddy North Sea floors and is sold as langoustine or scampi.

entities.name: Blue crab
entities.fact: The blue crab, the famous catch of the Gulf of Mexico and Chesapeake Bay, has invaded the Mediterranean, where it is now a serious pest.

entities.name: Stone crab
entities.fact: Stone crab fishers in Florida and the Gulf of Mexico twist off one claw and return the crab alive to regrow it.

entities.name: Dungeness crab
entities.fact: The Dungeness crab, named after a town in Washington State, is the prize crab fishery of the North American Pacific coast.

entities.name: Brown crab
entities.fact: The brown crab, with its pie-crust shell edge, is the main crab caught in the North Sea and the one usually sold dressed in Britain.

entities.name: Brown shrimp
entities.fact: The brown shrimp burrows into North Sea sand flats by day and is the shrimp netted in the Wadden Sea and sold as potted shrimps.

entities.name: Shrimp
entities.fact: Shrimp moult their shells as they grow and can regrow lost legs and antennae at the next moult.

entities.name: Crab
entities.fact: Crabs can deliberately drop a trapped claw or leg at a special break point and regrow it over a few moults.

entities.name: Hermit crab
entities.fact: Hermit crabs protect their soft abdomens in empty snail shells and can regrow lost claws and legs when they moult.

entities.name: Fiddler crab
entities.fact: A male fiddler crab that loses its giant signalling claw regrows one, which is how the big claw can end up on either side.

entities.name: Mantis shrimp
entities.fact: The peacock mantis shrimp strikes with the acceleration of a bullet and can regrow a damaged smashing club at its next moult.

entities.name: Horseshoe crab
entities.fact: Horseshoe crabs are closer to spiders than crabs and have changed little in about 450 million years, and their blue blood is used to test medicines.

entities.name: Sally Lightfoot crab
entities.fact: The bright red Sally Lightfoot crab skitters over Galápagos lava rocks and picks ticks off resting marine iguanas.

entities.name: Red king crab
entities.fact: Red king crabs introduced to the Barents Sea by Soviet scientists in the 1960s have since marched along the Norwegian coast as an invasive species.

entities.name: Gooseneck barnacle
entities.fact: Gooseneck barnacles cling to wave-battered rocks of the Pacific Northwest on leathery stalks and are a delicacy in Spain and Portugal.

entities.name: Sea star
entities.fact: A sea star can regrow a lost arm, and some species can grow a whole new body from a single arm with part of the central disc.

entities.name: Sea urchin
entities.fact: Sea urchins graze algae with a five-toothed mouth called Aristotle's lantern and can regrow broken spines.

entities.name: Sea cucumber
entities.fact: A threatened sea cucumber can expel its own intestines at an attacker and then regrow them within weeks.

entities.name: Brittle star
entities.fact: Brittle stars shed arms so readily that they are named for it, and they regrow them from the central disc.

entities.name: Basket star
entities.fact: Basket stars unfurl branching arms at night to net plankton and regrow any branches that are bitten off.

entities.name: Sea lily
entities.fact: Sea lilies and feather stars are crinoids, a group that dominated ancient seas and still regrows arms snapped off by predators.

entities.name: Crown-of-thorns starfish
entities.fact: The crown-of-thorns starfish eats coral, can regrow lost arms, and its outbreaks have stripped large areas of the Great Barrier Reef and Indian Ocean reefs.

entities.name: Blue sea star
entities.fact: The blue Linckia sea star of Indo-Pacific reefs can regrow an entire body from one severed arm, a stage known as a 'comet'.

entities.name: Sunflower sea star
entities.fact: The sunflower sea star of the Pacific Northwest has up to 24 arms and was nearly wiped out by sea star wasting disease after 2013.

entities.name: Ochre sea star
entities.fact: The ochre sea star of the Pacific Northwest keeps mussels from taking over the shore, the original 'keystone species'.

entities.name: Long-spined sea urchin
entities.fact: A mystery disease killed about 95 percent of Caribbean long-spined sea urchins in 1983, letting algae overgrow the reefs.

entities.name: Purple sea urchin
entities.fact: Purple sea urchins have multiplied along the Californian coast since sea stars died off, mowing down kelp forests into 'urchin barrens'.

entities.name: Red sea urchin
entities.fact: The red sea urchin of the Pacific coast of North America can live for more than 100 years and is harvested for its roe, sold as uni.

entities.name: Sea anemone
entities.fact: Sea anemones are animals that catch prey with stinging tentacles and can regrow from fragments, which is how some species clone themselves.

entities.name: Giant green anemone
entities.fact: The giant green anemone of Pacific Northwest tide pools gets its colour from algae living in its tissues.

entities.name: Sea fan
entities.fact: Sea fans are colonies of tiny coral polyps growing as flat, flexible fans set across the current to catch drifting food.

entities.name: Sea pen
entities.fact: Sea pens are feather-shaped coral colonies anchored in soft mud that glow green when touched, and fossils show the group is ancient.

entities.name: Brain coral
entities.fact: Brain corals build grooved domes that can live for centuries on Caribbean reefs.

entities.name: Elkhorn coral
entities.fact: Elkhorn coral, once the main reef builder of the Caribbean, is critically endangered after disease and bleaching destroyed most colonies.

entities.name: Staghorn coral
entities.fact: Staghorn coral is critically endangered in the Caribbean, where white band disease wiped out most of it from the 1980s onwards.

entities.name: Coral
entities.fact: Corals are colonies of tiny animals, and broken fragments can regrow into new colonies, which is how reef restoration nurseries work.

entities.name: Sponge
entities.fact: A sponge pushed through a sieve can reassemble itself, and whole sponges regrow from small fragments.

entities.name: Comb jelly
entities.fact: Comb jellies row through the water with beating rows of tiny cilia and can regrow their entire body from a fragment.

entities.name: Immortal jellyfish
entities.fact: The immortal jellyfish can turn its adult body back into a polyp and start life again, regenerating every tissue.

entities.name: Moon jellyfish
entities.fact: The moon jellyfish, with its four pale rings, drifts in huge blooms through the North Sea and Baltic in summer.

entities.name: Lion's mane jellyfish
entities.fact: The lion's mane jellyfish of cold northern seas can trail tentacles tens of metres long, making it the longest animal known.

entities.name: Portuguese man o' war
entities.fact: The Portuguese man o' war is not one animal but a colony, and its gas-filled float carries it across the Gulf of Mexico and Atlantic on the wind.

entities.name: Cannonball jellyfish
entities.fact: The cannonball jellyfish of the Gulf of Mexico is harvested, dried and exported to Asia as food.

entities.name: Sea squirt
entities.fact: Sea squirts are our closest invertebrate relatives, and colonial species can regrow entire bodies from a scrap of blood vessel.

entities.name: Christmas tree worm
entities.fact: Christmas tree worms live in tubes bored into Caribbean corals and snap their spiral crowns back inside when a shadow passes.

entities.name: Bobbit worm
entities.fact: The bobbit worm lurks buried in sand with only its jaws showing and ambushes fish at night, growing up to about 3 metres long.

entities.name: Marine flatworm
entities.fact: Marine flatworms cut into pieces can regrow into complete animals, and some are decorated as brightly as the nudibranchs they mimic.

entities.name: Ribbon worm
entities.fact: Ribbon worms fire a sticky proboscis to catch prey, and some species regrow a complete worm from a small fragment.

entities.name: Sea slug
entities.fact: Sea slugs include nudibranchs that store stinging cells from the anemones they eat and use them in their own defence.

entities.name: Elysia sea slug
entities.fact: The sea slug Elysia marginata can shed its own head, which then regrows an entire new body, heart included, within weeks.

entities.name: Goldfish
entities.fact: Goldfish were bred from dull carp in China about a thousand years ago, and released pets now grow huge and invasive in lakes around the world.

entities.name: Rainbow trout
entities.fact: The rainbow trout, native to Pacific coast rivers of North America, has been stocked on every continent except Antarctica and is invasive in many of them.

entities.name: Brown trout
entities.fact: The brown trout was carried from Europe to rivers worldwide by Victorian anglers and now displaces native fish from New Zealand to Patagonia.

entities.name: Brook trout
entities.fact: The brook trout of eastern North American streams is actually a char and shows white-edged fins and red spots ringed with blue.

entities.name: Lake trout
entities.fact: Lake trout live in cold deep lakes of North America and can live for decades and weigh more than 30 kilograms.

entities.name: Golden trout
entities.fact: The golden trout, California's state fish, lives in high Sierra Nevada streams and is coloured brilliant gold and red.

entities.name: Arctic char
entities.fact: The Arctic char is the northernmost freshwater fish, living in icy lakes and rivers of the Arctic and prized by fly anglers.

entities.name: Grayling
entities.fact: The grayling, 'lady of the stream', carries a tall sail-like dorsal fin and lives only in clean, cold rivers.

entities.name: Atlantic salmon
entities.fact: Atlantic salmon hatch in rivers, grow at sea, and return to their birth river to spawn, with the Baltic and Norwegian stocks among the most important.

entities.name: Chinook salmon
entities.fact: The chinook, or king salmon, is the largest Pacific salmon and the main food of the Pacific Northwest's resident orcas.

entities.name: Sockeye salmon
entities.fact: Sockeye salmon turn brilliant red with green heads when they return to spawn in the rivers of Alaska and British Columbia.

entities.name: Coho salmon
entities.fact: Coho salmon run up Pacific Northwest rivers in autumn and are prized by anglers for their acrobatic fight.

entities.name: Pink salmon
entities.fact: The pink salmon is the smallest and most abundant Pacific salmon and lives on a strict two-year cycle.

entities.name: Largemouth bass
entities.fact: The largemouth bass is the most popular game fish in the United States and has become invasive in lakes from Japan to Spain.

entities.name: Smallmouth bass
entities.fact: The smallmouth bass prefers cooler, rockier rivers and lakes than its largemouth cousin and fights hard for its size.

entities.name: Striped bass
entities.fact: Striped bass run up Atlantic coast rivers to spawn, and surf anglers pursue them from New England to the Carolinas.

entities.name: White bass
entities.fact: White bass are silver schooling fish of North American lakes and rivers that boil at the surface when chasing shad.

entities.name: Black sea bass
entities.fact: Black sea bass of the US Atlantic coast start life as females and later change into males.

entities.name: Sea bass
entities.fact: The European sea bass, sold as branzino, is a prized angling fish of the North Sea and Atlantic coasts and is widely farmed in the Mediterranean.

entities.name: Northern pike
entities.fact: The northern pike is an ambush hunter of weedy lakes and rivers, and it even lives in the brackish coastal waters of the Baltic Sea.

entities.name: Muskellunge
entities.fact: The muskellunge, 'fish of ten thousand casts', is the largest pike and can top 1.5 metres in the lakes of the Great Lakes region.

entities.name: Walleye
entities.fact: The walleye's reflective eyes let it hunt in dim lake water at dusk and night, and it is the favourite eating fish of the northern US and Canada.

entities.name: Zander
entities.fact: The zander is Europe's largest perch relative and lives in rivers, lakes and the brackish Baltic Sea.

entities.name: Yellow perch
entities.fact: The yellow perch, with its dark vertical bars, is the fish most children in North America catch first from a lake.

entities.name: European perch
entities.fact: The European perch lives in lakes and rivers and in the brackish Baltic Sea, and has become invasive in Australia as the redfin.

entities.name: Bluegill
entities.fact: The bluegill, a small sunfish of North American ponds, is named for the blue sheen on its gill cover.

entities.name: Pumpkinseed
entities.fact: The pumpkinseed sunfish is a brightly coloured pond fish of North America that has become invasive across Europe.

entities.name: Black crappie
entities.fact: Crappie are schooling sunfish of North American lakes, and anglers catch them in numbers around sunken brush in spring.

entities.name: Channel catfish
entities.fact: The channel catfish is the most fished catfish in North America and tastes the water with taste buds covering its whole body.

entities.name: Blue catfish
entities.fact: The blue catfish is North America's largest catfish, topping 60 kilograms, and has become invasive in Chesapeake Bay rivers.

entities.name: Wels catfish
entities.fact: The wels catfish of European rivers can exceed 2.5 metres and has been filmed lunging onto gravel banks to grab pigeons.

entities.name: Mekong giant catfish
entities.fact: The Mekong giant catfish is among the largest freshwater fish, reaching about 3 metres, and is critically endangered.

entities.name: Common carp
entities.fact: The common carp, spread from Asia and Europe to waters worldwide, is one of the most damaging invasive fish, muddying lakes as it roots in the bottom.

entities.name: Koi
entities.fact: Koi are ornamental common carp bred in Japan, and prized fish have sold for more than a million dollars.

entities.name: Silver carp
entities.fact: The silver carp, an Asian carp invading the Mississippi River system, leaps metres out of the water when startled by boat motors.

entities.name: Bighead carp
entities.fact: The bighead carp escaped from US fish farms in the 1970s and now dominates stretches of the Mississippi and Illinois rivers.

entities.name: Grass carp
entities.fact: The grass carp was imported to eat pond weeds and has since spread through rivers across the United States and beyond.

entities.name: Asian carp
entities.fact: Asian carp, a group of imported Chinese carp species, have overrun the Mississippi basin, and electric barriers try to keep them out of the Great Lakes.

entities.name: Tilapia
entities.fact: Tilapia are African river and lake fish farmed worldwide, and escaped stocks have become invasive across the tropics.

entities.name: Nile perch
entities.fact: The Nile perch, introduced to Lake Victoria in the 1950s, grows to about 2 metres and drove hundreds of native cichlid species to extinction.

entities.name: Red snapper
entities.fact: The red snapper is the signature fish of the Gulf of Mexico, where it gathers around reefs and oil platforms and can live about 50 years.

entities.name: Yellowtail snapper
entities.fact: The yellowtail snapper, with a bright yellow stripe and tail, follows snorkellers over Caribbean reefs hoping for food.

entities.name: Vermilion snapper
entities.fact: The vermilion snapper is a small red snapper relative of the Gulf of Mexico and Caribbean often sold as 'beeliner'.

entities.name: Snapper
entities.fact: Snappers are named for the way they snap their jaws when hauled on board, and they school around Caribbean reefs.

entities.name: Grouper
entities.fact: Groupers swallow prey whole with a sudden gulp of their huge mouths and many change sex from female to male as they grow.

entities.name: Nassau grouper
entities.fact: The Nassau grouper is critically endangered because fishers targeted the huge spawning gatherings where it was easiest to catch.

entities.name: Goliath grouper
entities.fact: The goliath grouper of the Gulf of Mexico and Caribbean can weigh over 300 kilograms and booms loudly at divers who come too close.

entities.name: Red grouper
entities.fact: The red grouper digs pits in the Gulf of Mexico seabed that become homes for dozens of other species.

entities.name: Gag grouper
entities.fact: The gag grouper is a favourite of Gulf of Mexico anglers and is often caught over rocky ledges and wrecks.

entities.name: Giant sea bass
entities.fact: The giant sea bass of California and Baja can top 2 metres and was fished to critically endangered levels before protection in 1982.

entities.name: Bluefin tuna
entities.fact: Atlantic bluefin tuna are warm-blooded, cross the Atlantic in weeks, and spawn in the Gulf of Mexico and Mediterranean.

entities.name: Southern bluefin tuna
entities.fact: The southern bluefin tuna of the Indian and Southern oceans is endangered after decades of overfishing for sushi markets.

entities.name: Yellowfin tuna
entities.fact: Yellowfin tuna, with their long yellow fins, travel with dolphin schools in the eastern Pacific and are a top game fish.

entities.name: Skipjack tuna
entities.fact: The skipjack is the most heavily fished tuna, and the Maldives still catch it one at a time with poles and lines.

entities.name: Blackfin tuna
entities.fact: The blackfin tuna is the smallest tuna and lives only in the western Atlantic, Caribbean and Gulf of Mexico.

entities.name: Dogtooth tuna
entities.fact: The dogtooth tuna is not a true tuna but a bonito relative with large conical teeth, prized by spearfishers on Indian Ocean reefs.

entities.name: Atlantic mackerel
entities.fact: Atlantic mackerel swim in vast schools through the North Sea in summer and must keep moving to breathe.

entities.name: King mackerel
entities.fact: The king mackerel is a fast, toothy game fish of the Gulf of Mexico that can top 1.5 metres.

entities.name: Spanish mackerel
entities.fact: The Spanish mackerel, spotted with gold, migrates along the Gulf of Mexico coast in spring and autumn.

entities.name: Wahoo
entities.fact: The wahoo is one of the fastest fish in the sea, and sport anglers prize its screaming first run.

entities.name: Blue marlin
entities.fact: The blue marlin, the fish of Hemingway's The Old Man and the Sea, can exceed 4 metres and is the dream catch of big-game anglers.

entities.name: White marlin
entities.fact: The white marlin is a smaller billfish of the Atlantic and Gulf of Mexico that anglers release after tagging.

entities.name: Black marlin
entities.fact: The black marlin of the Indo-Pacific can top 700 kilograms and is pursued off the Great Barrier Reef by big-game anglers.

entities.name: Striped marlin
entities.fact: Striped marlin hunt in packs, raising their stripes to glow bright blue as they corral baitfish.

entities.name: Sailfish
entities.fact: The sailfish raises a huge dorsal fin to herd sardines and is among the fastest fish, a prize for anglers in the Gulf of Mexico and Indian Ocean.

entities.name: Swordfish
entities.fact: Swordfish hunt squid at depth by day and rise toward the surface at night, warming their eyes and brain to see in the dark.

entities.name: Mahi-mahi
entities.fact: The mahi-mahi grows at an astonishing rate, lives only a few years, and flashes gold, green and blue when hooked.

entities.name: Tarpon
entities.fact: The tarpon, the 'silver king' of the Gulf of Mexico and Caribbean, leaps spectacularly when hooked and can gulp air from the surface.

entities.name: Bonefish
entities.fact: The bonefish is the 'grey ghost' of Caribbean sand flats, where fly anglers stalk it in water barely knee-deep.

entities.name: Permit
entities.fact: The permit is a wary, deep-bodied flats fish of the Caribbean that fly anglers consider among the hardest to catch.

entities.name: Snook
entities.fact: The snook lurks in Gulf of Mexico mangroves and under docks, and anglers prize its black lateral line and hard strike.

entities.name: Red drum
entities.fact: The red drum, or redfish, carries a black spot on its tail and became so popular as blackened redfish that Gulf of Mexico stocks had to be protected.

entities.name: Black drum
entities.fact: The black drum of the Gulf of Mexico makes a loud croak with its swim bladder and crushes oysters with its throat teeth.

entities.name: Spotted seatrout
entities.fact: The spotted seatrout is a drum, not a trout, and is the most caught game fish in the Gulf of Mexico.

entities.name: Sheepshead
entities.fact: The sheepshead of the Gulf of Mexico has eerily human-looking teeth for crunching barnacles and crabs off pilings.

entities.name: Cobia
entities.fact: The cobia follows rays and sharks through the Gulf of Mexico and fights hard enough to be a favourite of sight-casting anglers.

entities.name: Greater amberjack
entities.fact: The greater amberjack hangs over Gulf of Mexico wrecks and reefs and is nicknamed 'reef donkey' for its stubborn fight.

entities.name: Yellowtail amberjack
entities.fact: The yellowtail amberjack is a prized game fish off California, Baja and Australia and is served as hamachi in sushi bars.

entities.name: Giant trevally
entities.fact: The giant trevally of Indian Ocean reefs has been filmed leaping to snatch terns out of the air, and anglers prize its brutal strength.

entities.name: Roosterfish
entities.fact: The roosterfish of the eastern Pacific raises a comb of seven long dorsal spines and is caught from the beaches of Baja and Costa Rica.

entities.name: Barramundi
entities.fact: The barramundi of northern Australia starts life as a male and later becomes female, moving between rivers and the sea.

entities.name: Peacock bass
entities.fact: The peacock bass is an Amazon cichlid, not a bass, and was released in Florida canals, where anglers now chase it.

entities.name: Golden dorado
entities.fact: The golden dorado of South American rivers is a brilliant gold predator that fly anglers travel to Argentina and Bolivia to catch.

entities.name: Taimen
entities.fact: The taimen, the largest salmonid, hunts in Mongolian and Siberian rivers, can exceed 1.5 metres, and is known as the 'river wolf'.

entities.name: Mahseer
entities.fact: The golden mahseer of Himalayan rivers was the prized game fish of British India and is now endangered.

entities.name: Goliath tigerfish
entities.fact: The goliath tigerfish of the Congo River has 32 dagger-like teeth and has been known to attack crocodiles.

entities.name: Arapaima
entities.fact: The arapaima of the Amazon reaches about 3 metres and must surface to gulp air every few minutes.

entities.name: Murray cod
entities.fact: The Murray cod is Australia's largest freshwater fish, growing well over a metre in the Murray-Darling rivers.

entities.name: Alligator gar
entities.fact: The alligator gar of the Mississippi and Gulf coast rivers can reach 3 metres, breathes air, and has ganoid scales once used as arrowheads.

entities.name: Electric eel
entities.fact: The electric eel of the Amazon is a knifefish, not an eel, and can discharge more than 600 volts.

entities.name: Piranha
entities.fact: The red-bellied piranha of the Amazon has a bite among the strongest for its size of any animal, but mostly scavenges and eats fins.

entities.name: European eel
entities.fact: The European eel is critically endangered, and every one of them hatches in the Sargasso Sea before crossing to European rivers.

entities.name: Atlantic cod
entities.fact: Atlantic cod once supported the North Sea's biggest fishery, and a single female can release several million eggs.

entities.name: Haddock
entities.fact: The haddock carries a dark 'thumbprint' on its side and is the fish of choice for fish and chips across Scotland and the North Sea coast.

entities.name: Whiting
entities.fact: Whiting is a small cod relative abundant in the North Sea and one of the most caught fish by British shore anglers.

entities.name: Saithe
entities.fact: The saithe, sold as coley, is a dark cod relative that schools in the North Sea and off Norway.

entities.name: Ling
entities.fact: The ling is a long, eel-like cod relative of deep North Sea and Atlantic waters that can reach about 2 metres.

entities.name: Plaice
entities.fact: The plaice, with orange spots on its brown back, is the most important flatfish of the North Sea fishery.

entities.name: Common sole
entities.fact: The Dover sole buries itself in North Sea sand by day and feeds at night, and takes its name from the Kent port that supplied London.

entities.name: Turbot
entities.fact: The turbot is a large, almost round flatfish of the North Sea and Baltic, prized by chefs for its firm white flesh.

entities.name: European flounder
entities.fact: The European flounder lives in the North and Baltic seas and swims far up rivers into fresh water.

entities.name: Dab
entities.fact: The dab is a small, rough-skinned flatfish that is one of the most abundant fish on the North Sea floor.

entities.name: Lemon sole
entities.fact: The lemon sole is not a sole but a flounder relative of the North Sea, with a small head and smooth, slimy skin.

entities.name: Pacific halibut
entities.fact: The Pacific halibut can weigh more than 200 kilograms, and 'barn door' halibut are the prize of Alaskan and British Columbian anglers.

entities.name: Monkfish
entities.fact: The monkfish lies on the North Sea floor waving a fleshy lure above its enormous mouth, and only its tail is sold in fishmongers.

entities.name: John Dory
entities.fact: The John Dory carries a dark 'thumbprint' said to be St Peter's and sneaks up on prey in the North Sea by turning its thin body edge-on.

entities.name: Atlantic wolffish
entities.fact: The Atlantic wolffish crushes sea urchins and crabs with its fangs and makes antifreeze proteins to survive cold North Sea winters.

entities.name: Lumpsucker
entities.fact: The lumpsucker clings to North Sea rocks with a sucker made from its pelvic fins, and its roe is sold as cheap caviar.

entities.name: Garfish
entities.fact: The garfish of the North Sea and Baltic has a needle-like beak and bones that are naturally green.

entities.name: Lesser weever
entities.fact: The lesser weever buries itself in North Sea beach sand with venomous spines raised, and stings bathers who tread on it.

entities.name: Three-spined stickleback
entities.fact: The three-spined stickleback lives in both fresh water and the brackish Baltic Sea, and the male builds a nest and guards the eggs.

entities.name: Viviparous eelpout
entities.fact: The viviparous eelpout of the North and Baltic seas gives birth to fully formed live young, rare among bony fish.

entities.name: Sea trout
entities.fact: The sea trout is a brown trout that goes to sea to feed, and anglers fish for it at night in rivers draining into the North and Baltic seas.

entities.name: Humphead wrasse
entities.fact: The humphead wrasse can reach 2 metres and is endangered because live fish are sold for banquets across Asia.

entities.name: Beluga sturgeon
entities.fact: The beluga sturgeon of the Caspian and Black seas, source of the most expensive caviar, is critically endangered and can exceed 5 metres.

entities.name: White abalone
entities.fact: The white abalone of California was the first marine invertebrate listed as endangered in the USA after divers stripped it from the reefs.

entities.name: Spotted handfish
entities.fact: The spotted handfish of Tasmania walks along the seabed on hand-like fins and is critically endangered, with only a few thousand left.

entities.name: Coelacanth
entities.fact: The coelacanth was thought extinct for 66 million years until a trawler landed one off South Africa in 1938, and it is critically endangered.

entities.name: Dusky shark
entities.fact: The dusky shark is endangered because it matures at about 20 years old and recovers very slowly from fishing.

entities.name: Chinese sturgeon
entities.fact: The Chinese sturgeon, which migrates between the sea and the Yangtze, is critically endangered since dams blocked its spawning grounds.

entities.name: Giant devil ray
entities.fact: The giant devil ray of the Mediterranean is endangered, giving birth to only one pup every year or two.

entities.name: Totoaba
entities.fact: The totoaba of the Gulf of California is poached for a swim bladder worth more than gold in China, and the nets also drown the vaquita.

entities.name: Megalodon
entities.fact: Megalodon, a shark perhaps 15 to 20 metres long, died out roughly 3.6 million years ago, and its teeth are the size of a human hand.

entities.name: Plesiosaur
entities.fact: Plesiosaurs were long-necked marine reptiles that flew through the water on four flippers and vanished with the dinosaurs 66 million years ago.

entities.name: Elasmosaurus
entities.fact: Elasmosaurus had a neck of more than 70 vertebrae, and its first describer famously mounted the skull on the wrong end.

entities.name: Pliosaur
entities.fact: Pliosaurs were short-necked, huge-headed marine reptiles whose bite was among the most powerful of any animal that ever lived.

entities.name: Liopleurodon
entities.fact: Liopleurodon was a Jurassic pliosaur of European seas with a skull well over a metre long, far smaller than the 25-metre giant once shown on television.

entities.name: Kronosaurus
entities.fact: Kronosaurus was a Cretaceous pliosaur from Australia and Colombia whose skull alone measured over 2 metres.

entities.name: Ichthyosaur
entities.fact: Ichthyosaurs were dolphin-shaped reptiles that gave birth to live young at sea, and Mary Anning found the first complete skeleton in 1811.

entities.name: Shonisaurus
entities.fact: Shonisaurus was a Triassic ichthyosaur the size of a bus, and dozens of its skeletons lie together at Berlin-Ichthyosaur State Park in Nevada.

entities.name: Mosasaur
entities.fact: Mosasaurs were giant sea lizards related to monitor lizards and snakes that ruled the late Cretaceous seas until the asteroid struck.

entities.name: Tylosaurus
entities.fact: Tylosaurus, a mosasaur up to about 13 metres long, rammed prey with its bony snout in the shallow sea that once covered Kansas.

entities.name: Archelon
entities.fact: Archelon was the largest turtle ever, about 4 metres long, and swam the inland sea of Cretaceous North America.

entities.name: Trilobite
entities.fact: Trilobites crawled the seafloor for about 270 million years and were among the first animals with complex eyes before dying out 252 million years ago.

entities.name: Ammonite
entities.fact: Ammonites were coiled-shelled relatives of squid that filled the seas for over 300 million years and vanished with the dinosaurs.

entities.name: Belemnite
entities.fact: Belemnites were squid-like animals with an internal bullet-shaped shell, and their fossils were once thought to be thunderbolts.

entities.name: Sea scorpion
entities.fact: Sea scorpions, or eurypterids, were armoured arthropods that died out about 250 million years ago, and the largest reached about 2.5 metres.

entities.name: Anomalocaris
entities.fact: Anomalocaris was the top predator of the Cambrian seas about 500 million years ago, a metre-long hunter with grasping front limbs and a circular mouth.

entities.name: Hallucigenia
entities.fact: Hallucigenia, a spiny Cambrian worm from the Burgess Shale, was so strange that scientists first reconstructed it upside down.

entities.name: Opabinia
entities.fact: Opabinia, a Cambrian sea creature with five eyes and a clawed trunk, reportedly drew laughter when first shown to scientists in 1972.

entities.name: Dunkleosteus
entities.fact: Dunkleosteus was an armoured fish of the Devonian seas that sliced prey with bony blades instead of teeth.

entities.name: Placoderm
entities.fact: Placoderms, the first jawed fish, wore bony armour on their heads and vanished entirely about 360 million years ago.

entities.name: Leedsichthys
entities.fact: Leedsichthys was a Jurassic filter-feeding fish perhaps 16 metres long, the largest bony fish known to have lived.

entities.name: Xiphactinus
entities.fact: Xiphactinus was a 5-metre fanged fish of the Cretaceous, and one famous fossil contains a whole 2-metre fish swallowed just before it died.

entities.name: Helicoprion
entities.fact: Helicoprion was a shark relative with a spiral 'buzzsaw' of teeth in its lower jaw that puzzled scientists for more than a century.

entities.name: Stethacanthus
entities.fact: Stethacanthus was a small shark of about 360 million years ago whose males carried a flat, anvil-shaped dorsal fin topped with tooth-like scales.

entities.name: Cladoselache
entities.fact: Cladoselache is one of the earliest well-known sharks, preserved in Devonian shales around Cleveland, Ohio, about 370 million years old.

entities.name: Otodus
entities.fact: Otodus obliquus was a giant mackerel shark of about 50 million years ago whose lineage led to megalodon.

entities.name: Cretoxyrhina
entities.fact: Cretoxyrhina, the 'ginsu shark', was a 7-metre Cretaceous shark whose bite marks are found on mosasaur and plesiosaur bones.

entities.name: Conodont
entities.fact: Conodonts were eel-like early vertebrates known mainly from tiny tooth-like fossils, which geologists use to date rocks.

entities.name: Rudist
entities.fact: Rudists were strange cone-shaped clams that built reefs in Cretaceous seas and died out along with the dinosaurs.

entities.name: Basilosaurus
entities.fact: Basilosaurus was an early whale about 18 metres long with tiny hind legs, and its name means 'king lizard' because it was first mistaken for a reptile.

entities.name: Dorudon
entities.fact: Dorudon was a 5-metre early whale whose skeletons lie by the hundred in Egypt's Wadi Al-Hitan, the Valley of the Whales.

entities.name: Livyatan
entities.fact: Livyatan was a sperm whale of about 12 million years ago with teeth more than 30 centimetres long, named after Moby-Dick's author.

entities.name: Steller's sea cow
entities.fact: Steller's sea cow, a 9-metre relative of the dugong, was discovered in the Bering Sea in 1741 and hunted to extinction within 27 years.

entities.name: Caribbean monk seal
entities.fact: The Caribbean monk seal, noted by Columbus in 1494, was last seen in 1952 and declared extinct in 2008.

entities.name: Japanese sea lion
entities.fact: The Japanese sea lion bred on the coasts of Japan and Korea until hunting wiped it out, with the last confirmed sighting in the 1950s.

entities.name: Sea mink
entities.fact: The sea mink, a large coastal mink of New England and Atlantic Canada, was trapped to extinction for its fur by about 1900.

entities.name: Great auk
entities.fact: The great auk, a flightless North Atlantic seabird, was the original 'penguin', and the last known pair was killed on an Icelandic island in 1844.

entities.name: Labrador duck
entities.fact: The Labrador duck, a sea duck of the North American Atlantic coast, was the first bird endemic to North America to go extinct, last seen in 1878.

entities.name: Baiji
entities.fact: The baiji, the Yangtze river dolphin, was declared functionally extinct in 2006 after a survey of the whole river found none.

entities.name: Smooth handfish
entities.fact: The smooth handfish of Tasmania was declared extinct in 2020, the first modern marine bony fish to be lost, known from a single specimen collected in 1802.

entities.name: Regal blue tang
entities.fact: The regal blue tang, Dory in Finding Nemo, carries a sharp scalpel-like spine on each side of its tail and lives on Indo-Pacific reefs.

entities.name: Atlantic blue tang
entities.fact: The Atlantic blue tang of Caribbean reefs is bright yellow as a juvenile and turns deep blue as it grows.

entities.name: Yellow tang
entities.fact: The yellow tang, a brilliant lemon-yellow surgeonfish from Hawaii, is one of the most popular marine aquarium fish.

entities.name: Bluefish
entities.fact: Bluefish hunt in savage packs along the US Atlantic coast and will keep biting even after they are full.

entities.name: Blue shark
entities.fact: The blue shark is a slender, deep-blue ocean wanderer that crosses the Atlantic and is the most heavily fished shark in the world.

entities.name: Blue whiting
entities.fact: The blue whiting is a small cod relative of the deep North Atlantic caught in huge quantities for fishmeal and surimi.

entities.name: Lionfish
entities.fact: The lionfish, a venomous Indo-Pacific native, was released from aquariums off Florida and has invaded the whole Caribbean and Gulf of Mexico.

entities.name: Red mullet
entities.fact: The red mullet feels for food in the sand with two chin barbels and was so prized by the Romans that single fish sold for fortunes.

entities.name: Grey mullet
entities.fact: The grey mullet grazes algae and mud in estuaries and harbours around the world, and its roe is pressed into bottarga.

entities.name: Orange roughy
entities.fact: The orange roughy lives on deep seamounts and can live more than 150 years, which is why its fisheries collapsed so quickly.

entities.name: White sturgeon
entities.fact: The white sturgeon of the Fraser and Columbia rivers is North America's largest freshwater fish, reaching about 6 metres.

entities.name: Red gurnard
entities.fact: The red gurnard walks over the North Sea floor on finger-like fin rays and grunts audibly when caught.

entities.name: Bluestripe snapper
entities.fact: The bluestripe snapper, yellow with four blue stripes, schools in hundreds on Indian Ocean and Red Sea reefs.

entities.name: Yellow boxfish
entities.fact: The yellow boxfish juvenile is a bright yellow cube with black spots, and the species inspired an aerodynamic Mercedes concept car.

entities.name: White seabass
entities.fact: The white seabass of the Californian coast is a large drum, not a bass, and is a prize for kayak anglers in the kelp beds.

entities.name: Silver dollar
entities.fact: The silver dollar is a flat, coin-shaped Amazon fish kept in aquariums, a plant-eating cousin of the piranha.

entities.name: Black ghost knifefish
entities.fact: The black ghost knifefish swims backwards as easily as forwards by rippling one long fin and senses its world with a weak electric field.

entities.name: Blue cod
entities.fact: The blue cod is not a cod but a sandperch found only around New Zealand, where it is the favourite catch of shore anglers.

entities.name: Black molly
entities.fact: The black molly is a jet-black aquarium strain of a Central American livebearer that gives birth to free-swimming fry.

entities.name: Parrotfish
entities.fact: Parrotfish grind coral with beak-like teeth and excrete the remains as white sand, so much of a Caribbean beach has passed through a parrotfish.

entities.name: Stoplight parrotfish
entities.fact: The stoplight parrotfish of the Caribbean changes from a red-bellied female to a green male with a yellow spot on its gill cover.

entities.name: Angelfish
entities.fact: Marine angelfish are flat, brightly coloured reef fish with a sharp spine on the gill cover that separates them from butterflyfish.

entities.name: Queen angelfish
entities.fact: The queen angelfish of the Caribbean wears a blue-ringed 'crown' on its forehead and nibbles sponges along the reef.

entities.name: French angelfish
entities.fact: French angelfish swim Caribbean reefs in faithful pairs, black with yellow-edged scales, and juveniles clean larger fish.

entities.name: Damselfish
entities.fact: Damselfish farm patches of algae on the reef and fearlessly nip snorkellers and even sharks that drift too close to their gardens.

entities.name: Sergeant major
entities.fact: The sergeant major, a damselfish with five black bars like a sergeant's stripes, swarms around snorkellers on every Caribbean reef.

entities.name: Yellowtail damselfish
entities.fact: The juvenile yellowtail damselfish of the Caribbean is dark blue sprinkled with electric-blue spots, earning it the name jewelfish.

entities.name: Great barracuda
entities.fact: The great barracuda hangs motionless near Caribbean reefs and follows snorkellers out of curiosity, attracted by shiny objects.

entities.name: Moray eel
entities.fact: Moray eels hunt at night and have a second set of jaws in their throat that shoots forward to drag prey down.

entities.name: Green moray
entities.fact: The green moray of the Caribbean is actually brown; a yellow mucus coating makes it look green, and it can reach 2.5 metres.

entities.name: Trumpetfish
entities.fact: The trumpetfish hangs head-down among Caribbean sea rods and shadows larger fish to sneak up on prey.

entities.name: Squirrelfish
entities.fact: Squirrelfish hide in Caribbean reef caves by day and come out at night to hunt, using their huge eyes to see in the dark.

entities.name: Queen triggerfish
entities.fact: The queen triggerfish of the Caribbean blows jets of water to flip sea urchins over and eat their soft undersides.

entities.name: Porkfish
entities.fact: The porkfish, a yellow-striped grunt with two black bars on its head, schools under Caribbean ledges by day and feeds at night.

entities.name: French grunt
entities.fact: French grunts shelter in dense schools on Caribbean reefs by day and spread out over the sand at night to feed.

entities.name: Bluehead wrasse
entities.fact: The bluehead wrasse of the Caribbean starts life yellow and can turn into a blue-headed male within days if the dominant male disappears.

entities.name: Hogfish
entities.fact: The hogfish roots through Caribbean sand with its pig-like snout and is a favourite target of spearfishers.

entities.name: Smooth trunkfish
entities.fact: The smooth trunkfish of the Caribbean is a spotted triangular box of bone that blows jets of water into the sand to uncover worms.

entities.name: Honeycomb cowfish
entities.fact: The honeycomb cowfish of Caribbean reefs has two horns over its eyes and a boxy body patterned like a honeycomb.

entities.name: Porcupinefish
entities.fact: The porcupinefish inflates into a spiny ball when threatened and is a common sight peering out from Caribbean ledges.

entities.name: Scrawled filefish
entities.fact: The scrawled filefish drifts over Caribbean reefs scribbled with blue lines and spots, and can change its colours to match the background.

entities.name: Peacock flounder
entities.fact: The peacock flounder of the Caribbean lies on the sand covered in blue rings and can change its pattern within seconds.

entities.name: Spotted drum
entities.fact: The spotted drum of the Caribbean has a tall ribbon-like dorsal fin as a juvenile and hides under ledges by day to feed at night.

entities.name: Royal gramma
entities.fact: The royal gramma, purple in front and yellow behind, hovers upside-down under Caribbean ledges and is a favourite aquarium fish.

entities.name: Yellowhead jawfish
entities.fact: The yellowhead jawfish of the Caribbean lives in a burrow it digs in the sand, and the male broods the eggs in his mouth.

entities.name: Blue chromis
entities.fact: The blue chromis hovers in shimmering clouds above Caribbean reefs, picking plankton from the current.

entities.name: Needlefish
entities.fact: Needlefish skim just under the surface over Caribbean shallows and can leap out of the water at speed.

entities.name: Glassy sweeper
entities.fact: Glassy sweepers pack Caribbean caves in coppery schools by day and stream out at night to feed on plankton.

entities.name: Cushion sea star
entities.fact: The cushion sea star is the big orange starfish of Caribbean seagrass beds, often stacked up by snorkellers for photos.

entities.name: Ocean sunfish
entities.fact: The ocean sunfish is the heaviest bony fish and is often seen off the Galápagos being cleaned of parasites by reef fish.

entities.name: Galápagos bullhead shark
entities.fact: The Galápagos bullhead shark is a small spotted shark that rests on the rocks by day and crunches crabs and molluscs at night.

entities.name: King angelfish
entities.fact: The king angelfish, dark blue with a white bar and orange tail, runs cleaning stations for hammerheads around the Galápagos.

entities.name: Galápagos garden eel
entities.fact: Galápagos garden eels live in colonies of burrows on sandy slopes, swaying in the current like grass and vanishing when divers approach.

entities.name: Pacific seahorse
entities.fact: The Pacific seahorse, the largest seahorse at up to 30 centimetres, clings to black coral and sea fans in the Galápagos.

entities.name: Galápagos grouper
entities.fact: The Galápagos grouper, known locally as bacalao, is found almost only around the islands and is the most valued fish of the local fishery.

entities.name: Razor surgeonfish
entities.fact: The razor surgeonfish grazes the rocky shores of the Galápagos in huge grey schools with bright yellow tails.

entities.name: Red-lipped batfish
entities.fact: The red-lipped batfish of the Galápagos walks on the sand on leg-like fins, sporting bright red lips and a lure on its head.

entities.name: Zebra mussel
entities.fact: Zebra mussels arrived in the Great Lakes in ships' ballast water from the Black and Caspian seas in the 1980s and now clog pipes across North America.

entities.name: Quagga mussel
entities.fact: The quagga mussel followed the zebra mussel into the Great Lakes and has largely replaced it, carpeting the lake beds in their trillions.

entities.name: Northern snakehead
entities.fact: The northern snakehead, an air-breathing predator from Asia, was found in a Maryland pond in 2002 and has since spread through Potomac River tributaries.

entities.name: Sea lamprey
entities.fact: The sea lamprey invaded the Great Lakes through shipping canals and devastated lake trout by rasping into fish with its sucker mouth.

entities.name: European green crab
entities.fact: The European green crab has invaded both coasts of North America, Australia and South Africa, digging up eelgrass and eating young clams.

entities.name: Chinese mitten crab
entities.fact: The Chinese mitten crab, named for its furry claws, has invaded the Thames, the Elbe and San Francisco Bay, burrowing into riverbanks.

entities.name: Round goby
