entities.fact: The round goby from the Black and Caspian seas arrived in the Great Lakes in ballast water in 1990 and now numbers in the billions there and in the Baltic.

entities.name: Walking catfish
entities.fact: The walking catfish escaped from Florida fish farms in the 1960s and wriggles across wet ground between ponds, breathing air.

entities.name: Pacific oyster
entities.fact: The Pacific oyster, farmed worldwide, has escaped to build sharp-edged reefs on the Wadden Sea mudflats of the North Sea and in Australia.

entities.name: Caulerpa taxifolia
entities.fact: Caulerpa taxifolia, the 'killer alga', escaped from the Monaco aquarium in 1984 and carpeted thousands of hectares of the Mediterranean seabed.

entities.name: Wakame
entities.fact: Wakame, the kelp in miso soup, has spread from Japan to harbours in Europe, New Zealand, Australia and California on ship hulls.

entities.name: Sea walnut
entities.fact: The sea walnut, a comb jelly from the American Atlantic, reached the Black Sea in ballast water in the 1980s and ate so many fish eggs that the anchovy fishery collapsed.

entities.name: Killer shrimp
entities.fact: The killer shrimp, a large amphipod from the Black Sea region, has spread through Europe's canals to Britain, killing far more prey than it eats.

entities.name: Asian shore crab
entities.fact: The Asian shore crab turned up in New Jersey in 1988 and is now the most common crab on many rocky shores from Maine to North Carolina.

entities.name: Veined rapa whelk
entities.fact: The veined rapa whelk, a big predatory snail from Japan, invaded the Black Sea and later Chesapeake Bay, where it eats oysters and clams.

entities.name: Rabbitfish
entities.fact: Two rabbitfish species swam into the Mediterranean through the Suez Canal and have grazed the rocky reefs of the eastern Mediterranean bare of seaweed.

entities.name: Silver-cheeked toadfish
entities.fact: The silver-cheeked toadfish, a deadly poisonous puffer from the Red Sea, invaded the Mediterranean via the Suez Canal and bites through fishing nets and lines.

entities.name: New Zealand mud snail
entities.fact: The tiny New Zealand mud snail spreads on anglers' boots and can reach hundreds of thousands per square metre in rivers of the western USA and Europe.

entities.name: Asian clam
entities.fact: The Asian clam has spread through rivers across North America, South America and Europe and fouls the cooling systems of power stations.

entities.name: Mosquitofish
entities.fact: The mosquitofish was released worldwide to eat mosquito larvae and has instead wiped out native fish and frogs from Australia to Spain.

entities.name: Guppy
entities.fact: The guppy, the classic beginner's aquarium fish, now lives wild on every continent except Antarctica after releases to control mosquitoes.

entities.name: Red-eared slider
entities.fact: The red-eared slider, the pet-shop turtle, has been dumped into ponds worldwide and is now one of the most widespread invasive reptiles.

entities.name: American bullfrog
entities.fact: The American bullfrog, farmed for frogs' legs, has invaded ponds across Europe, Asia and the western USA, eating anything that fits in its mouth.

entities.name: Signal crayfish
entities.fact: The signal crayfish from North America has spread through European rivers, carrying a fungal plague that kills the native white-clawed crayfish.

entities.name: Plecostomus
entities.fact: The plecostomus, the aquarium 'algae eater', has been released into Florida, Texas and Mexican rivers, where its burrows collapse banks.

entities.name: Asian tiger shrimp
entities.fact: The Asian tiger shrimp, a farmed prawn up to 30 centimetres long, has escaped into the Gulf of Mexico and the south-eastern US coast.

entities.name: Common periwinkle
entities.fact: The common periwinkle, a European shore snail, was carried to Nova Scotia in the 1800s and now dominates rocky shores down to Chesapeake Bay.

entities.name: Siamese fighting fish
entities.fact: The Siamese fighting fish breathes air with a labyrinth organ, and the male builds a nest of bubbles and guards the eggs in it.

entities.name: Neon tetra
entities.fact: The neon tetra's electric blue stripe comes from tiny reflecting plates in its skin, and tens of millions are sold to aquarists each year.

entities.name: Cardinal tetra
entities.fact: The cardinal tetra, with red running the full length of its body, is still mostly caught wild in the Rio Negro for the aquarium trade.

entities.name: Clownfish
entities.fact: Clownfish are immune to their host anemone's sting, and every clownfish is born male, with the largest fish in a group becoming female.

entities.name: Freshwater angelfish
entities.fact: The freshwater angelfish is an Amazon cichlid with tall triangular fins that pairs for life and guards its eggs on a leaf.

entities.name: Oscar
entities.fact: The oscar is a big Amazon cichlid that recognises its owner, begs at the glass and rearranges the gravel in its tank.

entities.name: Molly
entities.fact: Mollies are hardy livebearers from Central America that thrive in anything from fresh to fully salty water.

entities.name: Platy
entities.fact: The platy is a small Mexican livebearer bred into dozens of colour forms and recommended for every beginner's tank.

entities.name: Swordtail
entities.fact: The male swordtail grows a long blade from the bottom of its tail that females prefer longer, a classic example of sexual selection.

entities.name: Zebrafish
entities.fact: The striped zebrafish of the aquarium trade became a star of science because its transparent embryos let researchers watch organs form.

entities.name: Corydoras
entities.fact: Corydoras are small armoured catfish from South America that gulp air at the surface and snuffle through aquarium gravel in groups.

entities.name: Discus
entities.fact: The discus is a round Amazon cichlid whose parents feed their fry on a mucus secreted from their own skin.

entities.name: Cichlid
entities.fact: Cichlids from Africa's Rift Valley lakes evolved into hundreds of species within one lake, and many brood their eggs in their mouths.

entities.name: Gourami
entities.fact: Gouramis breathe air with a labyrinth organ and feel their way with thread-like pelvic fins.

entities.name: Rainbowfish
entities.fact: Rainbowfish from New Guinea and Australia shimmer with shifting colours and are among the most peaceful community aquarium fish.

entities.name: Killifish
entities.fact: Some killifish live in puddles that dry up each year, surviving as eggs in the mud that hobbyists can buy and post in the mail.

entities.name: Tiger barb
entities.fact: The tiger barb from Sumatra and Borneo is a striped aquarium favourite that nips fins unless kept in a school of six or more.

entities.name: Cherry barb
entities.fact: The cherry barb, a small red fish from Sri Lankan streams, is far more common in aquariums than in the wild.

entities.name: Kuhli loach
entities.fact: The kuhli loach is a striped eel-like fish from South-east Asia that burrows into aquarium sand and comes out at night.

entities.name: Clown loach
entities.fact: The clown loach, orange with black bands, clicks audibly, sleeps on its side and can grow to 30 centimetres.

entities.name: Siamese algae eater
entities.fact: The Siamese algae eater is valued by aquarists because it is one of the few fish that eats stringy black beard algae.

entities.name: Otocinclus
entities.fact: Otocinclus are tiny suckermouth catfish from South America that graze algae off aquarium glass and plant leaves.

entities.name: Harlequin rasbora
entities.fact: The harlequin rasbora, with a black triangle on its side, lays its eggs on the underside of leaves in Malaysian and Thai streams.

entities.name: Ram cichlid
entities.fact: The ram cichlid is a small, brilliantly coloured dwarf cichlid from Venezuelan and Colombian streams that pairs up to guard its eggs.

entities.name: Convict cichlid
entities.fact: The convict cichlid, striped like a prison uniform, breeds so readily that it is used to study parental care in fish.

entities.name: Jack Dempsey
entities.fact: The Jack Dempsey cichlid from Central America was named after the boxer for its aggressive temper and strong-jawed face.

entities.name: Silver arowana
entities.fact: The silver arowana of the Amazon leaps up to 2 metres out of the water to snatch insects from branches and is kept by aquarists for luck.

entities.name: Mandarinfish
entities.fact: The mandarinfish is one of only two known vertebrates with true blue pigment, and it starves in aquariums unless given live food.

entities.name: Pea puffer
entities.fact: The pea puffer from Kerala in India is the smallest pufferfish, about 2.5 centimetres long, and hunts snails in the aquarium.

entities.name: Celestial pearl danio
entities.fact: The celestial pearl danio was discovered in a Myanmar pond in 2006 and became an aquarium sensation within months.

entities.name: Elephantnose fish
entities.fact: The elephantnose fish from African rivers senses its surroundings with a weak electric field and has one of the largest brains for its size of any fish.

entities.name: Glass catfish
entities.fact: The glass catfish of Thailand is so transparent that its spine and organs are plainly visible in the aquarium.

entities.name: Sturgeon
entities.fact: Sturgeons have rows of bony plates instead of scales and a skeleton largely of cartilage, a body plan little changed in about 200 million years.

entities.name: Lake sturgeon
entities.fact: The lake sturgeon of the Great Lakes and Mississippi can live for more than 100 years and does not breed until it is about 20.

entities.name: Paddlefish
entities.fact: The American paddlefish of the Mississippi swims with its mouth open to filter plankton and senses prey with its long electric-sensing paddle.

entities.name: Bowfin
entities.fact: The bowfin of eastern North American swamps can gulp air and is the last survivor of a fish order that flourished with the dinosaurs.

entities.name: Bichir
entities.fact: The bichir of African rivers has lungs, can crawl over land on its fins, and belongs to the most ancient living lineage of ray-finned fish.

entities.name: Lungfish
entities.fact: African lungfish survive the dry season buried in mud in a mucus cocoon, breathing air for months until the rains return.

entities.name: Australian lungfish
entities.fact: The Australian lungfish has barely changed in 100 million years and has one of the largest genomes of any animal yet sequenced.

entities.name: Burbot
entities.fact: The burbot is the only cod relative that lives in fresh water and spawns under the ice in midwinter.

entities.name: Barbel
entities.fact: The barbel is a bottom-feeding fish of fast European rivers, named for the four whiskers around its mouth.

entities.name: Tench
entities.fact: The tench, a slimy olive fish of still European waters, was once believed to heal other fish that rubbed against it.

entities.name: Roach
entities.fact: The roach, with its red fins and silver body, is the fish most often caught by beginners in European rivers and canals.

entities.name: Chub
entities.fact: The chub is a big-mouthed European river fish that will eat almost anything, from cherries to small fish.

entities.name: Candiru
entities.fact: The candiru is a tiny Amazon catfish that drinks blood from the gills of bigger fish and is the subject of lurid river legends.

entities.name: Giant freshwater stingray
entities.fact: A giant freshwater stingray caught in the Mekong in 2022 weighed about 300 kilograms, the heaviest freshwater fish ever recorded.

entities.name: Payara
entities.fact: The payara of the Orinoco and Amazon has two lower fangs so long that they fit into holes in its upper jaw.

entities.name: Hagfish
entities.fact: The hagfish, a jawless fish that has changed little in about 300 million years, can clog a predator's gills with buckets of slime in seconds.

entities.name: Chimaera
entities.fact: Chimaeras, or ratfish, split from the sharks about 400 million years ago and glide through deep water on wing-like fins with a venomous dorsal spine.

entities.name: Elephant shark
entities.fact: The elephant shark of Australia and New Zealand has the slowest-evolving genome of any vertebrate yet studied.

entities.name: Lingula
entities.fact: Lingula, a burrowing brachiopod on a fleshy stalk, looks much like fossils more than 450 million years old and was one of Darwin's original examples of a living fossil.

entities.name: Neopilina
entities.fact: Neopilina, a limpet-like deep-sea mollusc dredged up in 1952, belongs to a group thought extinct for 350 million years.

entities.name: Glass sponge
entities.fact: Glass sponges build skeletons of silica and have formed reefs since the Jurassic; living reefs survive off British Columbia.

entities.name: Lancelet
entities.fact: The lancelet, a finger-length fish-like animal that burrows in sand, has a body plan close to the ancestor of all vertebrates.

entities.name: Priapulid worm
entities.fact: Priapulid worms burrow in cold seafloor mud and look much as their relatives did in the Cambrian, more than 500 million years ago.

entities.name: Slit shell snail
entities.fact: Slit shell snails of deep tropical slopes belong to a lineage that first appeared more than 500 million years ago, and their shells are prized by collectors.

entities.name: Triops
entities.fact: Triops tadpole shrimp hatch in temporary pools from eggs that can wait years in dry dust, and their body plan dates back about 220 million years.

entities.name: Port Jackson shark
entities.fact: The Port Jackson shark of southern Australia lays spiral egg cases and belongs to the bullhead sharks, a group known from Jurassic fossils.

entities.name: Seahorse
entities.fact: Seahorses are fish whose males become pregnant, carrying the eggs in a belly pouch until they give birth to hundreds of tiny young.

entities.name: Sea snake
entities.fact: Sea snakes have paddle-shaped tails and venom stronger than most land snakes, and some never leave the water, giving birth at sea.

entities.name: Sea krait
entities.fact: The banded sea krait hunts eels on Indo-Pacific reefs but crawls ashore to digest, drink fresh water and lay its eggs.

entities.name: Sea cow
entities.fact: Sea cows, the manatees and dugong, are the only plant-eating marine mammals and are related to elephants rather than seals.

entities.name: Sea bream
entities.fact: The gilthead sea bream, named for the gold bar between its eyes, is one of the most farmed fish in the Mediterranean.

entities.name: Sea dragon
entities.fact: Sea dragons, seahorse relatives found only off southern Australia, drift among kelp disguised by leaf-like flaps of skin.

entities.name: Sea spider
entities.fact: Sea spiders have bodies so small that their guts and reproductive organs extend into their legs, and Antarctic species grow as wide as a dinner plate.

entities.name: Sea hare
entities.fact: The sea hare, a large sea slug with rabbit-ear tentacles, squirts purple ink when disturbed and is a classic animal for studying memory.

entities.name: Sea robin
entities.fact: Sea robins walk across the seabed on three finger-like fin rays that can taste the sand for buried prey, and they croak when caught.

entities.name: Sea wasp
entities.fact: The sea wasp, a box jellyfish of northern Australia, carries enough venom in its tentacles to kill a person within minutes.

entities.name: Sea nettle
entities.fact: Sea nettles trail long stinging tentacles and bloom in Chesapeake Bay and off California each summer, keeping swimmers out of the water.

entities.name: Sea butterfly
entities.fact: Sea butterflies are tiny swimming snails that flap wing-like feet, and their thin shells dissolve as the ocean turns more acidic.

entities.name: Sea angel
entities.fact: The sea angel is a shell-less swimming snail of cold seas that hunts sea butterflies by shooting out tentacles from its head.

entities.name: Sea pig
entities.fact: Sea pigs are pink deep-sea sea cucumbers that plod across abyssal mud on tube-feet legs, sometimes in herds of hundreds.

entities.name: Sea mouse
entities.fact: The sea mouse is a furry worm the size of a hand whose bristles shimmer with iridescent colours produced by natural photonic crystals.

entities.name: Sea apple
entities.fact: The sea apple is a round, brightly coloured sea cucumber of Indo-Pacific reefs that can poison an entire aquarium if it dies.

entities.name: Sea gooseberry
entities.fact: The sea gooseberry is a marble-sized comb jelly of North Atlantic waters that fishes with two long sticky tentacles.

entities.name: Sea moth
entities.fact: Sea moths are small armoured fish of Indo-Pacific sand flats that walk on their pelvic fins and spread wing-like pectoral fins.

entities.name: Sea raven
entities.fact: The sea raven is a lumpy, ragged-finned sculpin of the North American Atlantic coast that puffs itself up with water when caught.

entities.name: Sea pansy
entities.fact: The sea pansy is a flat, purple soft coral colony on sand that glows green when touched, thanks to a protein now used in laboratories.

entities.name: Sea whip
entities.fact: Sea whips are slender, unbranched soft coral colonies that sway on sandy seabeds of the Gulf of Mexico and US Atlantic coast.

entities.name: Sea toad
entities.fact: Sea toads, or coffinfish, are deep-sea anglerfish that can inflate their bodies with water and hold their breath for minutes to save energy.

entities.name: Sea louse
entities.fact: Sea lice are parasitic copepods that graze the skin of salmon and multiply in fish farms, where they are a major cause of losses.

entities.name: Sea snail
entities.fact: Sea snails range from tiny periwinkles to the giant triton, and many graze algae from rocks with a ribbon of teeth called a radula.

entities.name: Sea catfish
entities.fact: The hardhead sea catfish of the Gulf of Mexico is an angler's nuisance with venomous spines, and the male broods the eggs in his mouth.

entities.name: Atlantic herring
entities.fact: Atlantic herring form schools of billions in the North Sea and Baltic and communicate at night with bursts of bubbles from their vents.

entities.name: Pacific herring
entities.fact: Pacific herring spawn in such numbers along the North American Pacific coast that their milt turns whole bays milky white.

entities.name: Sardine
entities.fact: Sardines are small herring relatives that school in millions, and the famous South African 'sardine run' draws sharks, dolphins and gannets.

entities.name: Pacific sardine
entities.fact: The Pacific sardine fuelled Monterey's Cannery Row until the stock collapsed in the 1950s, and it still booms and busts with ocean cycles.

entities.name: Anchovy
entities.fact: Anchovies are small schooling fish with an underslung jaw, cured in salt since Roman times to make fish sauce.

entities.name: Peruvian anchoveta
entities.fact: The Peruvian anchoveta is the most heavily fished species on Earth, with catches that have exceeded 10 million tonnes in a single year.

entities.name: Northern anchovy
entities.fact: The northern anchovy schools along the North American Pacific coast and feeds everything from humpback whales to brown pelicans.

entities.name: Bay anchovy
entities.fact: The bay anchovy is probably the most abundant fish on the US Atlantic and Gulf of Mexico coasts, yet few people have ever seen one.

entities.name: Japanese anchovy
entities.fact: The Japanese anchovy supports one of the largest fisheries in East Asia and is dried whole as niboshi for making dashi stock.

entities.name: Menhaden
entities.fact: Menhaden are oily herring relatives caught by the hundreds of thousands of tonnes off the US coast for fishmeal and omega-3 oil, not for eating.

entities.name: Gulf menhaden
entities.fact: The Gulf menhaden is the biggest fishery by weight in the Gulf of Mexico and the main food of its pelicans, dolphins and redfish.

entities.name: Capelin
entities.fact: Capelin roll onto Newfoundland and Icelandic beaches in their millions to spawn, feeding cod, whales and puffins.

entities.name: Sprat
entities.fact: The sprat is a small herring relative abundant in the North Sea and Baltic, smoked and tinned as brisling sardines.

entities.name: Smelt
entities.fact: Smelt are small silver fish that smell of cucumber and run up streams in spring, where they are dipped out with nets.

entities.name: Sand lance
entities.fact: Sand lances bury themselves in the seabed at night and are the main food of North Sea puffins, kittiwakes and porpoises.

entities.name: American shad
entities.fact: The American shad, the largest herring, runs up Atlantic coast rivers each spring and was once the most valuable fishery on the US East Coast.

entities.name: Alewife
entities.fact: The alewife, a river herring of the US Atlantic coast, invaded the Great Lakes and once washed up dead on Chicago's beaches in the millions.

entities.name: Blueback herring
entities.fact: The blueback herring runs up rivers from Florida to Nova Scotia each spring to spawn and is hard to tell from the alewife.

entities.name: Atlantic silverside
entities.fact: The Atlantic silverside is a small schooling fish of US Atlantic estuaries whose sex is decided by the water temperature its eggs develop in.

entities.name: Eulachon
entities.fact: The eulachon of the Pacific Northwest is so oily that a dried fish with a wick can be lit like a candle, hence its name candlefish.

entities.name: Round herring
entities.fact: Round herrings are slim schooling fish of warm seas including the Gulf of Mexico, caught as bait and for fishmeal.

entities.name: Atlantic thread herring
entities.fact: The Atlantic thread herring, named for a long trailing ray on its dorsal fin, schools along the Gulf of Mexico coast and is netted for bait.

entities.name: Mackerel scad
entities.fact: The mackerel scad is a small schooling jack of tropical waters that is a staple bait and food fish from Hawaii to the Caribbean.

entities.name: Jack mackerel
entities.fact: The Pacific jack mackerel is a schooling jack, not a true mackerel, caught off California and Chile in enormous quantities.

entities.name: Atlantic horse mackerel
entities.fact: The Atlantic horse mackerel is a schooling jack of the North Sea and eastern Atlantic with a line of bony scutes along its side.

entities.name: Sardinella
entities.fact: Sardinellas are small sardine-like fish that support huge fisheries off West Africa, where they are smoked and dried for food.

entities.name: Kilka
entities.fact: Kilka are tiny sprats of the Caspian and Black seas that once made up most of the Caspian catch before the comb jelly invasion.

entities.name: Pacific saury
entities.fact: The Pacific saury, grilled whole as sanma in Japan, schools across the North Pacific and is caught at night under bright lights.

entities.name: Lanternfish
entities.fact: Lanternfish rise from the deep in vast schools every night and may make up more than half of all fish by weight in the open ocean.

entities.name: Hilsa
entities.fact: The hilsa shad migrates from the Bay of Bengal into the Ganges delta to spawn and is the national fish of Bangladesh.

entities.name: Cisco
entities.fact: The cisco, or lake herring, schools in cold North American lakes and is a whitefish rather than a true herring.

entities.name: Grunion
entities.fact: Grunion ride the highest tides onto Californian beaches at night to spawn in the sand, and crowds come to catch them by hand.

entities.name: Lingcod
entities.fact: The lingcod of the North American Pacific coast is neither a ling nor a cod but a giant greenling, and its flesh is sometimes naturally blue.

entities.name: Rockfish
entities.fact: Pacific rockfish include more than 60 species along the North American coast, and the rougheye rockfish can live more than 200 years.

entities.name: Garibaldi
entities.fact: The bright orange garibaldi, California's state marine fish, fiercely guards a nest of red algae in the kelp forest.

entities.name: Wolf eel
entities.fact: The wolf eel of the Pacific Northwest is not an eel but a 2-metre wolffish that pairs for life in a rocky den and crushes sea urchins.

entities.name: Sablefish
entities.fact: The sablefish, sold as black cod, lives on the deep slopes off Alaska and British Columbia and can live more than 90 years.

entities.name: Surfperch
entities.fact: Surfperches of the North American Pacific coast give birth to fully formed live young, which is unusual for a marine fish.

entities.name: Cabezon
entities.fact: The cabezon is a big-headed sculpin of Pacific coast kelp beds whose eggs are poisonous to eat.

entities.name: Kelp greenling
entities.fact: The kelp greenling of the Pacific Northwest looks like two species, the male grey with blue spots and the female gold with brown freckles.

entities.name: Salmon shark
entities.fact: The salmon shark, a warm-blooded relative of the great white, hunts salmon off Alaska and British Columbia in water near freezing.

entities.name: Leopard shark
entities.fact: Leopard sharks gather in the warm shallows of San Diego's La Jolla every summer, where snorkellers can wade among them.

entities.name: Pacific sleeper shark
entities.fact: The Pacific sleeper shark drifts through deep cold water off Alaska and has been found with whole seals and even giant octopus in its stomach.

entities.name: Pacific lamprey
entities.fact: The Pacific lamprey climbs waterfalls with its sucker mouth on its way up Columbia River tributaries and is a traditional food of Native peoples.

entities.name: Pacific cod
entities.fact: The Pacific cod supports one of Alaska's largest fisheries and gathers in the Bering Sea and Gulf of Alaska in winter to spawn.

entities.name: Pacific spiny lumpsucker
entities.fact: The Pacific spiny lumpsucker is a golf-ball-sized fish of the Pacific Northwest that sticks to eelgrass and rocks with a suction disc.

entities.name: Plainfin midshipman
entities.fact: The plainfin midshipman of the Pacific coast hums all night to attract mates, loud enough to keep houseboat residents awake.

entities.name: Grunt sculpin
entities.fact: The grunt sculpin of the Pacific Northwest hops along the bottom on its fins and hides inside empty giant barnacle shells.

entities.name: Sarcastic fringehead
entities.fact: The sarcastic fringehead of the Californian coast defends its burrow by gaping an enormous fluorescent mouth at rivals.

entities.name: California sheephead
entities.fact: The California sheephead, a wrasse of the kelp forest, is born female and turns into a black-and-red male with a bulging forehead.

entities.name: Opalescent nudibranch
entities.fact: The opalescent nudibranch of Pacific Northwest tide pools stores stinging cells from the hydroids it eats in the orange tips of its back.

entities.name: Red rock crab
entities.fact: The red rock crab of the Pacific Northwest has big black-tipped claws strong enough to crush barnacles and snails.

entities.name: Soldierfish
entities.fact: Soldierfish are big-eyed red fish that hover in reef caves by day and spread out over the reef at night to hunt plankton and crustaceans.

entities.name: Cardinalfish
entities.fact: Cardinalfish shelter in coral branches and urchin spines by day, hunt tiny crustaceans at night, and the males brood the eggs in their mouths.

entities.name: Cookiecutter shark
entities.fact: The cookiecutter shark rises from the deep at night and bites neat round plugs of flesh out of tuna, whales and even submarines.

entities.name: Horn shark
entities.fact: The horn shark of the Californian coast rests in rocky crevices by day and crunches sea urchins at night, which can stain its teeth purple.

entities.name: Swell shark
entities.fact: The swell shark of the Pacific coast hunts at night, swallows water to double its size when threatened, and glows green under blue light.

entities.name: Epaulette shark
entities.fact: The epaulette shark walks across reef flats on its fins at night on the Great Barrier Reef and can survive hours with almost no oxygen.

entities.name: Wobbegong
entities.fact: The wobbegong, a flattened carpet shark of Australian reefs, lies camouflaged by day and ambushes fish and octopus at night.

entities.name: Brownbanded bamboo shark
entities.fact: The brownbanded bamboo shark of Indo-Pacific reefs hides in crevices by day and pokes its snout into sand at night for worms and crabs.

entities.name: Small-spotted catshark
entities.fact: The small-spotted catshark, the commonest shark around Britain, rests by day and hunts crabs and small fish across the seabed at night.

entities.name: Flashlight fish
entities.fact: Flashlight fish hide in reef caves by day and emerge on dark nights, blinking pouches of glowing bacteria under their eyes to find prey.

entities.name: Conger eel
entities.fact: The conger eel, which can reach 3 metres, lurks in wrecks and rock holes by day and hunts fish, crabs and octopus at night.

entities.name: Rice's whale
entities.fact: Rice's whale, recognised as a species only in 2021, lives nowhere but the Gulf of Mexico and numbers perhaps 50 to 100 animals.

entities.name: Gafftopsail catfish
entities.fact: The gafftopsail catfish of the Gulf of Mexico trails long sail-like fin filaments, and the male carries the eggs in his mouth for weeks.

entities.name: Gulf sturgeon
entities.fact: The Gulf sturgeon spends summers in rivers such as the Suwannee and winters in the Gulf of Mexico, and leaping fish have injured boaters.

entities.name: Tripletail
entities.fact: The tripletail floats on its side under buoys and weed in the Gulf of Mexico, pretending to be a drifting leaf.

entities.name: Atlantic croaker
entities.fact: The Atlantic croaker of the Gulf of Mexico croaks loudly by vibrating its swim bladder and is the most common catch from Gulf piers.

entities.name: Oyster toadfish
entities.fact: The oyster toadfish grunts a foghorn-like call to attract mates and once flew on the Space Shuttle for balance experiments.

entities.name: Bonnethead shark
entities.fact: The bonnethead, a small hammerhead of the Gulf of Mexico, is the only shark known to eat and digest seagrass.

entities.name: Florida pompano
entities.fact: The Florida pompano is caught in the Gulf of Mexico surf with sand fleas and is one of the most expensive fish on American menus.

entities.name: Southern flounder
entities.fact: The southern flounder of the Gulf of Mexico is speared at night by 'floundering' anglers wading the shallows with lights.

entities.name: Lesser electric ray
entities.fact: The lesser electric ray buries itself in Gulf of Mexico sand and can deliver a shock of up to about 37 volts.

entities.name: Ladyfish
entities.fact: The ladyfish, a small tarpon relative of the Gulf of Mexico, leaps and tumbles so wildly when hooked that anglers call it the poor man's tarpon.

entities.name: Bumphead parrotfish
entities.fact: The bumphead parrotfish, largest of its family at up to 1.3 metres, rams coral heads with its forehead and can eat about 5 tonnes of reef a year.

entities.name: Oriental sweetlips
entities.fact: The oriental sweetlips of Indian Ocean reefs hangs under ledges in striped schools by day, and its juveniles wriggle like poisonous flatworms.

entities.name: Titan triggerfish
entities.fact: The titan triggerfish of Indian Ocean reefs guards its nest in a cone-shaped territory and will chase and bite divers who swim over it.

entities.name: Powder blue tang
entities.fact: The powder blue tang is found only in the Indian Ocean, where it grazes reef flats in large schools from East Africa to the Maldives.

entities.name: Emperor angelfish
entities.fact: The emperor angelfish of Indo-Pacific reefs changes completely as it grows, from blue-and-white rings as a juvenile to yellow and blue stripes as an adult.

entities.name: Bluestreak cleaner wrasse
entities.fact: The bluestreak cleaner wrasse runs cleaning stations where bigger fish queue to have parasites picked off, and it can recognise itself in a mirror.

entities.name: Omura's whale
entities.fact: Omura's whale was only described in 2003, and the first living population studied was found off Madagascar in the Indian Ocean in 2015.

entities.name: Indian Ocean humpback dolphin
entities.fact: The Indian Ocean humpback dolphin lives in shallow coastal water from South Africa to India and is endangered by nets and coastal development.

entities.name: Spanish dancer
entities.fact: The Spanish dancer, a red nudibranch up to 40 centimetres long, swims through Indian Ocean reefs at night by rippling its mantle like a flamenco skirt.

entities.name: Harlequin shrimp
entities.fact: The harlequin shrimp of Indo-Pacific reefs eats nothing but starfish, which it flips over and slowly devours arm by arm.

entities.name: Ribbon eel
entities.fact: The ribbon eel, a moray of Indo-Pacific reefs, starts life black, turns electric blue as a male and finally yellow as a female.

entities.name: Indian mackerel
entities.fact: The Indian mackerel is the everyday fish of the Indian Ocean coast, schooling in the surface waters from East Africa to Indonesia.

entities.name: Southern right whale
entities.fact: Southern right whales calve in winter in the bays of South Africa and Western Australia, so close to shore that they can be watched from cliffs.

entities.name: Day octopus
entities.fact: The day octopus of Indo-Pacific reefs hunts in daylight, unlike most octopuses, changing colour and texture as it crawls over the coral.
